challenge.already-signed-in.goal.1: …and a token cache exists, so the provider is not queried on every request
challenge.already-signed-in.lesson: A valid session should not be lost when the provider that issued it goes down.
challenge.already-signed-in.hint.1: There are two critical findings, and they describe different problems. One states that 'Auth0' is a single point of failure; the other states that the call directed at it has no alternative when the provider does not respond.
challenge.already-signed-in.hint.2: An identity provider cannot be replicated, because it is not a component of yours. What can be decided is how the shop behaves while the provider is unavailable; and a session that is already open does not need to be validated again.
challenge.already-signed-in.hint.3: The fallback is declared on the call, in the inspector. Once it is set, take 'Auth0' down in Simulate mode: the provider still fails, but it no longer brings the shop down with it.
The shop still queries the provider, and knows what to respond when the provider is unavailable
With 'Auth0' down, no requests are lost
challenge.already-signed-in.story: The identity provider was unresponsive for twenty minutes. It was expected that no new users could sign in; what nobody expected was that users who were already signed in, with sessions open since the morning, could not continue buying either. The shop queries 'Auth0' on every request, so when 'Auth0' is unavailable, the shop is unavailable too.
challenge.already-signed-in.title: Not even the users already signed in
challenge.backlog.goal.1: …and no component exceeds 80 % of its capacity
challenge.backlog.lesson: A queue decouples in time, but it does not create capacity.
challenge.backlog.hint.1: Check the worker's utilisation and the backlog figure in the simulation panel. The queue is at 10 % of its capacity, yet it keeps filling up.
challenge.backlog.hint.2: A queue decouples in time, but it does not create capacity. The throughput of an asynchronous system is determined by the consumer, not by the queue.
challenge.backlog.hint.3: Several consumers on the same queue share the work among themselves. Once the worker is no longer the bottleneck, check which component behind it becomes the next one.
challenge.backlog.requirement.1: The entry point still handles 500 rps
challenge.backlog.requirement.2: No work accumulates in the queue
challenge.backlog.requirement.3: At least two consumers compete for the work
challenge.backlog.requirement.4: No worker runs more than two copies
challenge.backlog.requirement.5: Whatever cannot be processed is stored somewhere
challenge.backlog.requirement.6: And no incoming requests are rejected
challenge.backlog.story: The system accepts 500 orders per second and places them in a queue. The queue has no problem: it holds five thousand messages. The problem is the customer who has been waiting twenty minutes for a confirmation email, and tomorrow it will be a customer who has waited two hours. Queueing is not the same as processing.
challenge.backlog.title: The queue grows faster than it drains
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.goal.1: …and zone 'b' also holds one: the copies are distributed, not merely moved
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.lesson: Two copies in the same location fail together: redundancy is measured in locations, not in components.
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.hint.1: Open the inspector for 'Api' and for 'Api 2' and check the zone field. Then enter Simulate mode, take down the whole of zone 'a', and count how many components turn red.
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.hint.2: Two copies only count as two if they can fail independently. Sharing a location means sharing the outage: what matters is not the number of components, but the number of locations that would have to fail at once.
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.hint.3: A component's zone is set in its inspector, and changing it costs nothing: distributing capacity does not increase the bill. Bear in mind that the load balancer and the entry point are also located somewhere.
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.requirem: The entry point still handles 300 rps
If the whole of zone 'a' goes down, the entry point remains healthy
And zone 'a' still holds at least one component: emptying it is not the same as distributing
And each API declares its zone, and they are not the same
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.story:
The decision was right: two APIs behind a load balancer with health checks, and the shop survived a machine reboot. Then, on Thursday at 04:11, an entire aisle of the data centre lost power — zone 'a' — and the shop went down anyway, because both copies were in that aisle.

Every component already declares which zone it is in. Separate them, then take zone 'a' down again from Simulate mode.
challenge.both-in-the-same-zone.title: Both copies were in the same zone
challenge.database-overload.goal.1: …and the shop still responds if the database goes down
challenge.database-overload.lesson: Removing work is cheaper than adding capacity.
challenge.database-overload.hint.1: Check the utilisation shown on each component on entering Simulate mode: the figure shows which component cannot keep up.
challenge.database-overload.hint.2: The database does not need to see every request. Anything that was requested a moment ago can be answered without consulting it.
challenge.database-overload.hint.3: A cache only passes on the requests it cannot answer. With an 80 % hit ratio, only a fifth of the traffic reaches the database.
The entry point still handles 300 rps
No component exceeds 80 % of its capacity
And without spending more than 18 in total
And no incoming requests are rejected
And the cache waits for the origin on a miss
challenge.database-overload.story:
The shop receives 300 requests per second, and every one of them ends up querying the same database. The database handles 200. It is rejecting one request in three, and the ones it does serve take half a second.

The incoming traffic cannot be changed. Rearrange the architecture so the database is no longer over its capacity.
challenge.database-overload.title: The database cannot keep up
challenge.email-can-wait.goal.1: …and it survives the database going down too
challenge.email-can-wait.goal.2: …and no email is lost while 'Mailer' is down
challenge.email-can-wait.lesson: A call whose answer is not needed should not be waited for.
challenge.email-can-wait.hint.1: Take 'Mailer' down in Simulate mode and follow the arrow backwards: a failure propagates from the component that does not respond to the component that was waiting for it.
challenge.email-can-wait.hint.2: What determines whether a failure spreads is not the timeout, but whether anything is waiting for the response. It is worth considering what the customer actually needs for their order to be complete.
challenge.email-can-wait.hint.3: An asynchronous call returns nothing, so it cannot return an error either. Change the call's mode in the inspector.
challenge.email-can-wait.requirement.1: The shop continues selling while 'Mailer' is down
challenge.email-can-wait.requirement.2: The confirmation email does not block the customer
challenge.email-can-wait.story: Every order sends a confirmation email. On Tuesday the mail service was down for twenty minutes, and during those twenty minutes nobody could buy: orders were saved, payments went through, but each request remained blocked waiting for the email to be sent. The email is not the order.
challenge.email-can-wait.title: The email can wait
challenge.exposed-database.goal.1: …and no critical finding is left in the analyser
challenge.exposed-database.lesson: Securing a system is not about adding a component; it is about changing who can talk to whom.
challenge.exposed-database.hint.1: Check the Security area of the analysis: there are two critical findings, and they describe different problems. One asks whether the door is locked; the other asks whether there is a door at all.
challenge.exposed-database.hint.2: Securing a system is not about adding a security component: it is about changing who can talk to whom. Start with the arrow that should not exist.
challenge.exposed-database.hint.3: Everything that traffic reaches before passing through an API or a gateway is publicly exposed, and every exposed component that reaches the data must require credentials.
challenge.exposed-database.requirement.1: Nothing reaches the database without passing through another component first
challenge.exposed-database.requirement.2: Every entry point that reaches the data requires credentials
challenge.exposed-database.requirement.3: The data is still readable from the API
challenge.exposed-database.requirement.4: And no component that only routes traffic talks to the database
challenge.exposed-database.requirement.5: And the entry point still handles its 100 rps
challenge.exposed-database.story: A pentester sends a screenshot: they connected to the shop's PostgreSQL instance from their laptop. The connection string was in a public repository, but that is not the underlying problem: the problem is that there was something to connect to. The reporting dashboard that was plugged directly into the database a year ago left the door open.
challenge.exposed-database.title: The database is on the internet
challenge.flying-blind.goal.1: …and if telemetry goes down, no requests are lost
challenge.flying-blind.lesson: An observability component that is not connected observes nothing.
challenge.flying-blind.hint.1: Read the warning in the panel carefully: it does not say the component is missing; it says that nothing reaches it. Locate it on the canvas and count how many arrows go in or out of it.
challenge.flying-blind.hint.2: Observability is wired component by component: every unconnected component produces its own warning, so the area's score improves with each connection. Either direction counts: the component can push its metrics, or the telemetry can scrape them.
challenge.flying-blind.hint.3: Be careful how it is connected. If the call to telemetry waits for a response, the shop now depends on telemetry being available. Take 'Telemetry' down in Simulate mode and check the extra goal.
challenge.flying-blind.requirement.2: There is still an observability component to consult
challenge.flying-blind.story: On Thursday at seven in the evening the shop stopped selling. Word came from a dissatisfied customer forty minutes later, and determining which of the three components was failing took another twenty. The telemetry component has been on the diagram since day one: somebody drew it, and there it remained. Merely drawn, it observes nothing.
challenge.flying-blind.title: Flying blind
challenge.god-service.goal.1: …and if 'Payments' goes down, it takes less than a fifth of the architecture down with it
challenge.god-service.lesson: A cycle breaks when one of the two directions stops waiting.
challenge.god-service.hint.1: Check the Coupling area of the analysis. The figure that matters is not how many components there are, but how many each one calls.
challenge.god-service.hint.2: Reducing dependencies is not about moving them around: it is about 'Core' no longer needing to know about everything. Group related responsibilities behind the component that already owns them.
challenge.god-service.hint.3: Calls that need no response can go through a queue, and what goes through a queue stops being a deploy-time dependency. Likewise, the cycle only breaks when one of the two directions stops waiting.
challenge.god-service.requirement.1: No component calls more than three others directly
challenge.god-service.requirement.3: No component accumulates too many dependencies
challenge.god-service.story: 'Core' calls seven services. Every deployment of any of those seven requires testing 'Core', and 'Core' is deployed three times a day. Two of them call back into it, creating a cycle that nobody on the current team can explain. There is also a component that is not connected to anything.
challenge.god-service.title: A service that knows everything
challenge.it-does-not-fit.goal.1: …and without adding a single new component
challenge.it-does-not-fit.lesson: Throttling is not scaling: the limit protects what is behind it, but the rejected users are not served by anyone.
challenge.it-does-not-fit.hint.1: Observe the bar along the bottom edge of each component: it is the load meter. One of them is receiving more than it can handle, and the analysis states by how much.
challenge.it-does-not-fit.hint.2: There are two ways to clear a capacity warning: give more capacity to the component that cannot cope, or admit fewer requests. The second also works, which is why this challenge includes both checks.
challenge.it-does-not-fit.hint.3: The instance count is set in the component inspector, and the traffic dial at the bottom makes it possible to check how much load the design can handle before saving anything. The spare copies of one component can be reassigned to the component that falls short.
challenge.it-does-not-fit.requirement.1: The search engine still handles 500 rps
challenge.it-does-not-fit.requirement.2: The search engine is still present
challenge.it-does-not-fit.requirement.3: No component has less capacity than the load it carries
challenge.it-does-not-fit.requirement.4: And no incoming requests are rejected
challenge.it-does-not-fit.requirement.5: And at a lower cost than today: 24 at most
challenge.it-does-not-fit.story: The sale tripled search traffic, and the search service began to struggle. It did not go down — that would have been easier to detect: it kept responding, more and more slowly, until users grew tired and reloaded, which generated even more searches. The declared traffic is real, and it will still be there next week.
challenge.it-does-not-fit.title: It does not fit
challenge.latency-budget.lesson: Latency is not set by the processing. It is set by the queueing.
challenge.latency-budget.hint.1: A component at 100 % of its capacity takes twenty times longer to respond than an idle one. Latency is reduced with headroom, not with faster processing.
challenge.latency-budget.hint.2: Two things reduce a component's utilisation: receiving less load, or having more capacity.
challenge.latency-budget.hint.3: The database must remain, but it does not have to be on the path of every request.
challenge.latency-budget.requirement.1: The entry point still handles 300 rps
challenge.latency-budget.requirement.3: The catalogue responds in under 100 ms
challenge.latency-budget.requirement.4: And without spending more than 30 in total
challenge.latency-budget.requirement.5: And no call stops waiting for its response just to be faster
challenge.latency-budget.requirement.6: And no incoming requests are rejected
challenge.latency-budget.story:
The catalogue takes over 800 ms to respond under its current traffic. The target is under 100 ms.

The code has not changed and the machines cannot be upgraded: how long each component takes depends on how close it is to its capacity, and the database is on the path of every request. Removing it is not allowed.
challenge.latency-budget.title: 800 ms is too much
challenge.million-a-day.goal.1: …and the entry point limits the requests it accepts
challenge.million-a-day.lesson: Every component added also adds load to the database.
challenge.million-a-day.goal.2: …and something is monitoring the system when it fails
challenge.million-a-day.hint.1: Start by adding what the brief requests and evaluate again. The relevant part comes afterwards.
challenge.million-a-day.hint.2: The background processing queries the same database, so adding it pushes the database past its capacity.
challenge.million-a-day.hint.3: A database can handle more when it is not a single machine: read replicas multiply its capacity.
challenge.million-a-day.requirement.1: The entry point is sized for the peak: 116 rps
challenge.million-a-day.requirement.3: There is somewhere to store the files that are uploaded
challenge.million-a-day.requirement.5: No component exceeds 80 % of its capacity at peak
challenge.million-a-day.requirement.6: And the peak fits within a budget of 42
challenge.million-a-day.requirement.7: And no incoming requests are rejected at the peak
challenge.million-a-day.story:
The brief is to design an architecture for a million requests a day, with a REST API, PostgreSQL, authentication, file upload and background processing.

A million requests a day is 11.6 requests per second on average, which is very little. But requests do not arrive evenly: the peak is ten times the average, so the system must be sized for 116 rps. The gap between average and peak is half of this exercise.

The other half appears when the missing pieces are added.
challenge.million-a-day.title: A million requests a day
challenge.nobody-drains-it.goal.1: …and messages that cannot be processed do not simply vanish
challenge.nobody-drains-it.lesson: A queue does not call anyone: it delivers messages. The arrow must leave the queue.
challenge.nobody-drains-it.hint.1: The warning does not say that a worker is missing: it says that the arrow between 'Billing' and 'Invoices' points in the wrong direction. Select it on the canvas and examine both ends.
challenge.nobody-drains-it.hint.2: An arrow runs from the caller to the component that responds. A queue does not respond to calls: it delivers messages, so the arrow must leave the queue. Delete the arrow and draw it again, this time starting from the queue's port.
challenge.nobody-drains-it.hint.3: As soon as it is fixed, a warning will appear that could not be raised before: while nothing consumes the queue, the analyser cannot yet ask what happens to messages that fail along the way. That is the extra goal.
challenge.nobody-drains-it.story: At month-end close, not a single invoice went out. The billing worker has been running for three weeks with no errors in its log and nothing processed; the queue, meanwhile, has grown to sixty thousand messages. Nobody changed anything: the diagram has been like this from the start.
challenge.nobody-drains-it.title: Nothing consumes the queue
challenge.nobody-noticed.goal.1: …and no requests are lost with 'Catalog' down either
challenge.nobody-noticed.lesson: The blast radius is not the same as what the customer loses.
challenge.nobody-noticed.hint.1: Simulate a 'Products' outage and compare two figures that measure different things: how many components are affected, and what share of requests is lost. Fixing the first does not fix the second.
challenge.nobody-noticed.hint.2: A component's failure only stops spreading if its callers have an alternative. Without one, the caller goes down too, and then the caller's caller, all the way to the entry point. What determines whether the customer notices is not how many components are affected, but whether any path remains that can respond without them.
challenge.nobody-noticed.hint.3: Two mechanisms are needed, and both matter. One provides the alternative response when the target does not reply. The other stops calling the target as soon as it is known to be failing: without it, the alternative response arrives after the caller has already given up waiting.
challenge.nobody-noticed.requirement.1: The entry point still handles 300 rps
challenge.nobody-noticed.requirement.2: The product database is still present
challenge.nobody-noticed.requirement.3: The product page is still read at request time, not later
challenge.nobody-noticed.requirement.4: Every call to a database is synchronous and has a timeout
challenge.nobody-noticed.requirement.5: With 'Products' down, no requests are lost
challenge.nobody-noticed.requirement.6: 'Catalog' still reads from 'Products' at request time, not later
challenge.nobody-noticed.story: On Tuesday the product database was down for eleven minutes. The panel turned red everywhere, as expected. What nobody expected was that the shop would stop responding entirely: there is a cached product page and a 'not available' message written two years ago, and neither was ever used. Half the diagram in red is acceptable. Zero requests served is not.
challenge.nobody-noticed.title: Half of it goes down and nobody notices
challenge.no-new-hardware.goal.1: …and the shop responds in under 60 ms
challenge.no-new-hardware.lesson: Without new hardware, the only option left is changing where the requests go.
challenge.no-new-hardware.hint.1: The two usual levers do not fit in the budget: one more copy of the shop costs 4 and one database replica costs 10. The only thing that can be changed is where the requests go.
challenge.no-new-hardware.hint.2: Lowering a component's utilisation without adding capacity means less load must reach it. Another component has to respond on its behalf.
challenge.no-new-hardware.hint.3: For the optional goal: every hop in the chain adds its processing time and its network time. With the cache in front, it is worth considering whether the component in the middle is still needed.
challenge.no-new-hardware.requirement.1: The entry point still handles 350 rps
challenge.no-new-hardware.requirement.3: No component exceeds 80 % of its capacity
challenge.no-new-hardware.requirement.4: And the total cost does not exceed 18
challenge.no-new-hardware.requirement.5: And no incoming requests are rejected
challenge.no-new-hardware.story: The usual problem: 350 requests per second, the database and the catalogue above their capacity, and the shop taking almost a second to respond. The difference is that this quarter the budget is fixed at 18, and the current design already costs 18. Anything may be drawn as long as the bill does not increase. The only option left is changing the architecture's shape.
challenge.no-new-hardware.title: Fix it without buying hardware
challenge.payments-friday.goal.1: …and it survives the database going down too
challenge.payments-friday.lesson: Resilience lives in the calls, not in the list of components.
challenge.payments-friday.hint.1: Without a timeout, no other mechanism can act: the call does not fail, it simply never returns. Start there.
challenge.payments-friday.hint.2: A timeout bounds the wait, but on its own it protects nothing. What contains a failure is having an alternative when the destination does not respond.
challenge.payments-friday.hint.3: If the operation does not need an immediate response, the alternative is not to wait for it: an asynchronous call never propagates an outage backwards.
challenge.payments-friday.requirement.1: The shop still responds with 'Payments' down
challenge.payments-friday.requirement.2: Every call to a service is synchronous and has a timeout
challenge.payments-friday.requirement.4: And every call that no longer waits goes through a queue
challenge.payments-friday.requirement.5: The order still reaches the payment, directly or through a queue
challenge.payments-friday.story:
Every Friday afternoon, when the order peak arrives, the payment provider stops responding for a few minutes. The provider cannot be fixed. What can be done is to keep the shop working in the meantime: customers should be able to browse and order even if the charge has to wait.

Induce the failure in Simulate mode, observe which components go down with it, and correct the architecture.
challenge.payments-friday.title: The payment service goes down every Friday
challenge.reproduce-the-incident.lesson: A failure is not understood until it can be reproduced.
challenge.reproduce-the-incident.hint.1: This challenge is passed by building the problem, not by fixing it. Start by asking why the degradation stops at two components when only two are drawn.
challenge.reproduce-the-incident.hint.2: A slow component drags down whatever is waiting for it, and that component drags down the next. For the degradation to travel far, there must be a chain of components waiting on one another.
challenge.reproduce-the-incident.hint.3: The initial call is protected: it contains the failure instead of letting it through. Check which mechanisms it carries, and what changes if the chain drawn does not carry them.
challenge.reproduce-the-incident.require: The analyser reports a long synchronous chain
With 'Recommendations' degraded, at least three components degrade
No component calls more than two others directly
The reproduction stays at five components or fewer
challenge.reproduce-the-incident.story: A customer reports that their whole system degrades when their recommendations service becomes slow — only slow, never down. The starting diagram does not confirm it: with two components drawn, the degradation stops there. Reproduce it. Draw the smallest architecture in which this actually happens; filling the canvas does not count. If it takes half a company's worth of components to occur, that was not what was happening.
challenge.reproduce-the-incident.title: Reproduce what happened to the customer

challenge.retry-storm.goal.1: …and the customer receives a response in under one second
challenge.retry-storm.hint.1: Inject latency into 'Inventory' in Simulate mode and observe the request amplification. Compare it with the retries configured on each call.
challenge.retry-storm.hint.2: Retries multiply; they do not add: three levels with two retries each produce twenty-seven requests for every incoming one. Retrying at every hop means retrying the entire chain.
challenge.retry-storm.hint.3: Retry in one place only, and add a mechanism that stops calling a target once it is known to be failing. A long timeout is also part of the problem: it prolongs every attempt before giving up.
challenge.retry-storm.requirement.1: The entry point still handles 100 rps
challenge.retry-storm.requirement.2: Retries no longer multiply along the chain
challenge.retry-storm.requirement.3: With 'Inventory' slow, at most three requests are generated for each one coming in
challenge.retry-storm.requirement.4: Every call to a service is synchronous and has a circuit breaker
challenge.retry-storm.requirement.5: And no call stops waiting for its response without a queue in between
challenge.retry-storm.story: The inventory service stalled for three seconds over a two-minute window. It did not go down: it became slow. Yet the incident lasted forty minutes and brought down services that had nothing to do with it. The logs show twenty-seven times more requests than entered through the front door. The mechanism intended to survive failures was the one that caused the incident.
challenge.retry-storm.title: The retries brought the system down
challenge.single-point-of-failure.goal.1: …and it takes down less than half the architecture with it
challenge.single-point-of-failure.lesson: Redundancy must be drawn, and something must check which copies are still alive.
challenge.single-point-of-failure.hint.1: Enter Simulate mode, take down 'Api', and count how many components turn red. Everything behind it goes down as well, even though nothing happened to those components.
challenge.single-point-of-failure.hint.2: A component that everything else depends on is not corrected by making it larger: it is corrected by ensuring it is no longer the only one.
challenge.single-point-of-failure.hint.3: A load balancer distributes traffic across the copies behind it, but it only stops sending traffic to a failed copy if it checks their health.
challenge.single-point-of-failure.requir: The entry point still handles 150 rps
If 'Api' goes down, the entry point remains healthy
The Api is no longer a single machine
challenge.single-point-of-failure.story: The API runs on a single machine. It works. On Monday morning that machine rebooted on its own, and for nine minutes there was no shop: no catalogue, no basket, nothing. There is no budget for new hardware up front, so prove the solution first with the existing components, arranged differently. Induce the failure in Simulate mode and observe how far it spreads.
challenge.single-point-of-failure.title: Everything goes through one machine
challenge.third-party-outage.goal.1: …and when the provider is slow, the customer waits less than two seconds
challenge.third-party-outage.lesson: What is not yours cannot be corrected; it can only be contained.
challenge.third-party-outage.hint.1: Check the Resilience area. One finding only appears on calls to an external service, and it says something different from the finding raised for every other call.
challenge.third-party-outage.hint.2: With a component of your own there are three options: scale it, correct it, or contain it. With a third party's, only the third remains, which is why this component has no editable fields.
challenge.third-party-outage.hint.3: Containing is not about waiting less: it is about having a response available without the provider. For the optional goal, compare how long the timeout waits before giving up with how long the provider takes on its worst day.
challenge.third-party-outage.requirement: The entry point still handles 150 rps
The provider remains in the architecture
No call to an external service is left without an alternative
The shop keeps responding while 'Payments' is down
And the payment is not resolved by simply no longer waiting for the provider
The payment request still reaches the provider
challenge.third-party-outage.story: The payment provider is down for one hour per quarter, and its SLA allows it. It cannot be scaled, it does not accept a corrective deployment, and there is nobody to call to bring it back up. The only thing within reach is ensuring the shop no longer depends on the provider responding. Take 'Payments' down in Simulate mode and observe which components go down with it.
challenge.third-party-outage.title: The failing component is not yours
challenge.thirty-seconds.goal.1: …and with 'Orders' down, the customer is informed in under five seconds
challenge.thirty-seconds.lesson: A timeout does not protect the system: it decides how long the customer waits.
challenge.thirty-seconds.hint.1: The warning does not say that a timeout is missing: it says that the current one bounds nothing. From thirty seconds onwards the model abandons the call on its own, so a longer timeout offers exactly as much protection as none.
challenge.thirty-seconds.hint.2: A timeout is chosen based on what the call actually costs, not on intuition. The finding itself states what this call costs; a few times that figure is a reasonable value.
challenge.thirty-seconds.hint.3: The extra goal is not determined by the analyser but by the customer: take 'Orders' down in Simulate mode and check the latency under the fault. It equals the declared timeout exactly, and it is how long a customer will spend in front of a blank screen.
challenge.thirty-seconds.requirement.2: The call to 'Orders' is still synchronous and declares a timeout
challenge.thirty-seconds.requirement.3: And that timeout really does bound the wait
challenge.thirty-seconds.story: The call to the orders service has a sixty-second timeout because, years ago, somebody saw an unusual spike and raised it as a precaution. On Tuesday 'Orders' stopped responding, and the shop did not fail: it waited a full minute, request after request, until it ran out of connections. A minute is more than enough time for a customer to close the tab.
challenge.thirty-seconds.title: Thirty seconds is not a limit
challenge.timeout-was-enough.goal.1: …and no component is left operating near its capacity
challenge.timeout-was-enough.lesson: A timeout ages as the load grows.
challenge.timeout-was-enough.hint.1: Before modifying the timeout, check the load meters along the chain. No component is over its capacity, yet the call still takes more than a second. Compare what each component takes now with what it would take when idle.
challenge.timeout-was-enough.hint.2: A timeout does not describe the call: it describes how long one is willing to wait. The call's duration varies with the utilisation of everything behind it, and between 80 % and 100 % that multiplier quadruples. That is why the timeout that was adequate a year ago no longer is, and why a circuit breaker makes the call fail sooner without making it fit.
challenge.timeout-was-enough.hint.3: There are only two ways to lower a component's utilisation: add capacity, or send it less load. Reducing what the customer waits for has a third: stop making them wait for every link in the chain.
challenge.timeout-was-enough.requirement: The entry point still handles 600 rps
Every call to a service is still synchronous and still has a timeout
No call takes longer than its timeout allows
The customer receives a response in under 400 ms
No component runs more than four copies of itself
And no call is made asynchronous just to meet the target
And no incoming requests are rejected
challenge.timeout-was-enough.story: The one-second timeout between 'Edge' and 'Storefront' has been in place for a year and had never fired. Nobody has touched it. Since the spring campaign it fires on almost every request, and the team wants to raise it to five seconds. Raising it would make the customer wait five seconds instead of one: it fixes nothing; it merely takes longer to fail. What changed is not the timeout.
challenge.timeout-was-enough.title: The timeout that used to be enough
challenge.two-services-one-table.goal.1: …and without making any request travel a longer path
challenge.two-services-one-table.lesson: A schema is an interface: if two services write to it, they are coupled internally.
challenge.two-services-one-table.hint.1: The Coupling finding is not about a call: it is about two arrows ending at the same data store. The interface between those two services is not HTTP but the table — and nobody versions it.
challenge.two-services-one-table.hint.2: Mark one of the two calls as read-only in the inspector. The warning does not disappear, but its wording changes: with two writers the problem is ownership; with one writer and one reader, the problem is how changes are communicated.
challenge.two-services-one-table.hint.3: There are two legitimate solutions, and they do not cost the same. Giving each service its own data does not make any request travel further; querying the owner through its API does, and the extra goal will indicate it as soon as that is done.
challenge.two-services-one-table.require: The entry point still handles 80 rps
Every schema has a single owner
challenge.two-services-one-table.story: The billing team added a column on Thursday, and orders stopped being saved. Neither service shipped a faulty deployment and neither did anything unusual: both write to the same tables, so the schema is effectively the interface between them — an interface nobody versions, that appears in no contract, and that breaks without warning.
challenge.two-services-one-table.title: Two services, one table
challenge.who-is-calling.goal.1: …and no critical finding is left in the analysis
challenge.who-is-calling.lesson: An entry point that does not verify who is calling is not a real barrier.
challenge.who-is-calling.hint.1: The critical finding is in the Security area, and it is not about the database: it is about the entry point. Behind it sits data, and the entry point has no way of knowing who is calling.
challenge.who-is-calling.hint.2: Authentication is a checkbox on the entry component, in its inspector. Declaring it is not a formality: the analyser behaves differently depending on what is declared, and declaring the actual situation is the first requirement.
challenge.who-is-calling.hint.3: If the entry point genuinely cannot authenticate, the alternative is to place something in front of it that can — an API or a gateway — and allow only that component to talk to what is inside.
challenge.who-is-calling.story: The order form works correctly and has been in production for two years. What nobody had examined is that the API behind it verifies nothing: anyone who knows the address can place orders on someone else's behalf, and behind it sits the database with everyone's orders. Nobody has intruded yet, which is not the same as nobody being able to.
challenge.who-is-calling.title: Who is calling?
