export.prompt.baseline: The “Starting point” section is not what you are reviewing: it is the design's origin. Use it to understand what was attempted, and indicate whether the changes move in the right direction.
export.prompt.body:
You are a senior software architect. Above you have an architecture, its diagram and the
result of a deterministic analyser, with the simulation of a scenario if one was run.

The findings listed **are already true**: you do not need to rediscover them or question them.
What I am asking for is what the analyser cannot do:

1. Order them by what you would fix first, and explain why in that order.
2. Point out what the rules do **not** see: choice of technology, boundaries between services,
   naming, or risks that do not follow from the topology.
3. If some part of the design looks right to you even though the analyser penalises it, say so
   and argue it.

Be concrete and use the names of the components.

export.simulation.discarded.one: {count:number} fault pointed at elements that are no longer in the architecture and was not applied.
export.simulation.discarded.other: {count:number} faults pointed at elements that are no longer in the architecture and were not applied.

export.simulation.noFaults: **No faults injected**: this is how the architecture behaves at rest.

export.simulation.rest.one: The rest ({count:number} element) keeps working normally.
export.simulation.rest.other: The rest ({count:number} elements) keeps working normally.

export.simulation.unaffected: No component is affected: the architecture absorbs the whole scenario.
finding.ASYNC_NO_QUEUE.passed.explanatio: Every asynchronous call between the system's components goes through a queue or a topic: if the consumer is away, the message stays written and is picked up later.
finding.ASYNC_NO_QUEUE.passed.message: Every call that does not wait has a queue where its work can wait.
finding.ASYNC_NO_QUEUE.unbuffered.explan: Not waiting is acceptable: an outage of '{target}' does not block '{source}'. However, the message is not stored anywhere either. If '{target}' is down or saturated at that moment, the work is lost without notice, and '{source}' cannot retry it without storing it itself. A call that does not wait needs a place where the work can wait.
finding.ASYNC_NO_QUEUE.unbuffered.messag: '{source}' hands work to '{target}' without waiting and without a queue.
finding.ASYNC_NO_QUEUE.unbuffered.sugges: Draw a queue between '{source}' and '{target}' — or a topic if several components need the message: '{source}' publishes to it and '{target}' consumes from it. If the response is needed immediately, the call is synchronous: mark it as such and give it a timeout.
finding.CACHE_AS_STORE.noOrigin.explanat: No component that uses '{node}' reaches a database or an object storage, so the data it holds exists nowhere else. A cache makes no durability guarantees: after an eviction, a restart or a cold node the data is gone, with nowhere to rebuild it from. A cache that cannot be lost has ceased to be a cache.
finding.CACHE_AS_STORE.noOrigin.message: '{node}' is the only place its data lives.
finding.CACHE_AS_STORE.noOrigin.suggesti: Place a system of record behind it — with the cache in front or alongside — and let the cache be what it is: a copy that can be lost. If the data really is ephemeral (sessions, counters), this design is acceptable; it is worth indicating that in the component's name.
finding.CACHE_AS_STORE.passed.explanatio: Everything a cache holds also exists in a system of record, so losing it costs latency and not data.
finding.CACHE_AS_STORE.passed.message: Every cache has an origin behind it.
finding.CYCLE.detected.explanation: None of the components involved can be deployed, started or recovered on its own. If the cycle is synchronous, one of them going down blocks the rest.
finding.CYCLE.detected.suggestion.decoup: The asynchronous hop already avoids the deadlock, but the mutual dependency is still there: neither of them can be deployed or versioned without the other. Invert one of the directions, or move what they share into a third component.
finding.CYCLE.detected.suggestion.shared: The cycle runs through a component that holds state, so this is not a wiring problem: two components are governing the same data. Give that data a single owner and have the other components request it from that owner. Inserting a queue would remove the deadlock but leave the shared ownership in place.
finding.CYCLE.detected.suggestion.synchr: Break the cycle with an asynchronous hop: have one of the steps publish an event instead of waiting for an answer. While every call blocks, a failure in any one of the components blocks the rest.
finding.CYCLE.passed.explanation: The dependencies between components were followed and none doubles back on itself: they can all be deployed and started in some order.
finding.EXPOSED_DATABASE.passed.explanat: Reaching the data requires going through an API or a gateway first, which is where the caller's identity can be checked.
finding.EXPOSED_DATABASE.reachable.expla: Outside traffic reaches the data directly, so there is no place to check who is calling or what they are requesting.
finding.EXPOSED_DATABASE.reachable.messa: '{node}' can be reached without going through any API.
finding.EXPOSED_DATABASE.reachable.sugge: Place an API or a gateway in front, and allow only that component to talk to the data.
finding.EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK.noTimeout.e: '{target}' is not a component of yours: it cannot be scaled, it cannot be given a corrective deployment, and there is no telling when it will recover. The call also has no timeout: if the provider hangs, '{source}' waits indefinitely, and without that limit no other mechanism can act.
finding.EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK.noTimeout.s: Bound the wait with a timeout and decide what to respond when the provider is unavailable — a fallback — or stop calling it while it is down with a circuit breaker. If the operation needs no immediate response, move it out of the customer's request.
finding.EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK.passed.expl: Every synchronous call to a third party knows what to do when the third party does not respond.
finding.EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK.passed.mess: No external dependency can bring the system down.
finding.EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK.unprotected: '{target}' is not a component of yours: it cannot be scaled, it cannot be given a corrective deployment, and there is no telling when it will recover. A timeout bounds the wait, but when it fires there is still no response and the request fails all the same.

Decide what to respond when the provider is unavailable — a fallback — or stop calling it while it is down with a circuit breaker. If the operation needs no immediate response, move it out of the customer's request.
finding.HIGH_COUPLING.fanOut.explanation: A component that needs that many pieces to work is hard to deploy, test and reason about in isolation, and its availability is the product of all of theirs.
A component of this kind does not usually originate this many dependencies. Check that the arrows point the right way: the convention is that the source depends on the target.

Fanning out is this component's job, so the number by itself is not the problem. What is worth checking is that it has not accumulated business logic of its own; and if different clients need different things, one BFF per client is cheaper than a single entry point that knows everything.

Check whether some of those responsibilities belong in the component itself, or whether part of the calls could become asynchronous events. Its availability is the product of the availability of everything it needs in order to respond.
finding.HIGH_COUPLING.passed.explanation: The number of components each one depends on was counted, and none needs so many that it becomes hard to deploy or test on its own.
finding.HIGH_COUPLING.passed.message: No component piles up too many dependencies.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.passed.me: Every arrow joins two things that can talk to each other.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.passed.ex: Every arrow was checked at both ends to confirm it describes a call that can actually happen: no store calls anyone, no component of the system calls the users, the CDN talks to an origin, and the scheduler triggers work.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.store.mes: '{source}' is a store, and a call leaves it towards '{target}'.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.store.exp: A database or a bucket is a destination: it stores what it receives and answers whoever queries it; it does not call anyone. This arrow is almost always drawn backwards — the intended meaning is that '{target}' reads from or writes to '{source}'.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.store.sug: Reverse the arrow. If the store genuinely originates the call — a trigger, a change stream, a replication — leave it as it is: this notice raises a question; it does not assert an error.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.client.ex: The outside is where requests come from, not where they go: nothing in the system calls a user's browser. This arrow is usually the response drawn as if it were a call. Outgoing webhooks do exist, but their destination is another system, and they are drawn as an external service.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.client.su: Reverse the arrow: it is the user who calls '{source}'. If it is a genuine push (notifications, websockets), leave it: this notice raises a question; it does not assert an error.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.cdn.expla: A CDN serves content from its origin: an API, a gateway, a balancer, a service, a bucket or somebody else's origin. It runs no queries and publishes no messages, so this arrow describes nothing that can happen — and what the analysis computes about '{target}' through it is an answer to a question nobody asked.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.cdn.sugge: Put what actually serves the content behind the CDN (the API, the gateway or the bucket) and let that be what talks to '{target}'. It is a diagram mistake, and until it is fixed the rest of the panel describes an architecture other than yours.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.scheduler: A scheduler triggers work: a worker, a service, an API, somebody else's service, or a queue that hands it to somebody. There is no work to trigger at '{target}' — you do not schedule a call to the users, to a CDN, or to a store with nobody there to do anything with it.

Draw what carries out the work when the clock fires — usually a worker — and let that be what talks to '{target}'. If the clock genuinely calls there, leave it: this notice raises a question; it does not assert an error.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.asyncClie: '{source}' calls '{target}' without waiting for the answer.

The client is the one who waits: every request that comes in from outside has someone watching the screen until it returns. An asynchronous arrow from the outside does not describe a possible call, and with the box unticked the loss of '{target}' stops affecting the users, which is exactly what the analysis has to measure.

Mark the call from '{source}' to '{target}' as synchronous. What the user fires and does not wait for — a background upload, a notification — is born inside the system, in the component that receives it, and goes from there to a queue.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.asyncDoor: '{source}' takes requests from outside and waits for nobody.

It is an entry point: its caller is outside, watching a screen until the response arrives. Yet every call it makes is declared as non-waiting, so there is nothing to respond with — and the work was not placed in a queue to be done later either. With those boxes unticked, the model counted all those requests as served and the loss of anything behind the door affected nobody; in reality, this entry point serves none of them.

Mark as synchronous the call '{source}' responds with: the one that brings back what the client requested. If the work really is done later, place a queue in between and let '{source}' respond “received”: queueing is accepting; not waiting is not responding.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.asyncRout: '{source}' forwards to '{target}' without waiting for the answer.

A router does no work of its own: it forwards a request whose client is waiting on the other side, and returns whatever '{target}' responds. An asynchronous arrow from a gateway, a load balancer or a CDN does not describe a possible call: nobody collects that response. In addition, with the box unticked, the loss of '{target}' stops propagating and the diagram appears to survive an outage it does not survive.

Mark the call from '{source}' to '{target}' as synchronous and give it a timeout. If there really is work that needs no answer, it does not leave from the router: it leaves from the component that processes it, towards a queue.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.asyncIden: '{source}' asks '{target}' who is calling, and does not wait for the answer.

Authentication is a question and an answer: '{source}' cannot let anyone through until '{target}' responds. An asynchronous arrow to an identity provider does not describe authentication: it describes a request that gets in without anyone having verified its identity. In addition, with the box unticked, the loss of '{target}' affects nothing, which is exactly what an identity dependency cannot afford.
Mark the call from '{source}' to '{target}' as synchronous, with a timeout, and decide what '{source}' answers when the provider is away: a fallback for those already signed in, or a token cache.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.asyncCach: The cache '{source}' resolves its misses against '{target}' without waiting.

A cache answers with what it holds and, when it does not hold the data, queries the origin and waits for it: a cache miss is synchronous by definition. An asynchronous arrow from '{source}' to '{target}' does not describe a cache: it describes one that responds empty and updates later. In addition, with the box unticked, '{target}' can go down without the diagram registering it.
Mark the call from '{source}' to '{target}' as synchronous, with a timeout. To survive the origin going down, give it a fallback: serving what the cache holds is exactly that.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.asyncRead: '{source}' reads from '{target}' without waiting for the data.

The call does not declare a write — and an undeclared access counts as a read — while also declaring that it does not wait for the response. Both cannot be true: reading means waiting for the data. Deferred writes do exist — the change is recorded somewhere and applied later — but they are declared as writes and require a queue in between. In addition, with the box unticked, the loss of '{target}' stops counting in everything the analysis measures.
Mark the call from '{source}' to '{target}' as synchronous and give it a timeout. If it is a write that can wait, declare the access as a write and put a queue between the two.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.routerFal: '{source}' declares a fallback towards '{target}', and has nothing to answer with.

A gateway or a load balancer routes requests: when '{target}' does not respond, there is no cached page and no “unavailable” message that '{source}' could return instead. The checkbox claims an alternative response exists, and here there is none; the model no longer trusts it — it neither serves requests with it nor discounts the dependency — and while it is ticked, the diagram promises a containment that does not exist.

Remove the fallback from '{source}' → '{target}'. What contains the loss of '{target}' behind a router is another copy to route to, with a health check; the fallback, if there is one, lives in whoever processes the request.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.writeFall: '{source}' declares a fallback for a write to '{target}'.

The call declares a write, and a write that does not happen cannot be approximated: there is no stale value to return, and no cached page can stand in for an order that was not saved. The checkbox claims an alternative response exists, and the model no longer trusts it — it neither serves the request with it nor discounts the single point of failure — so while it is ticked, the diagram promises a containment that does not exist.

Remove the fallback from '{source}' → '{target}'. What protects a write is a timeout and a circuit breaker, to fail fast; and if it can wait, a queue in between where the work waits for '{target}' to come back.
finding.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.routerToD: A gateway or a load balancer routes requests; it does not run SQL. Whatever queries a database is an API or a service — and is therefore an entry point that must require authentication and be counted as such. While a router talks to the database, the analysis treats a component that only routes as if it were a guarded entry point.

Put an API or a service between '{source}' and '{target}': it is what queries and what authenticates. If '{source}' is really the panel doing the query, change its type to API and declare its authentication.
finding.MISSING_CACHE.direct.explanation: The whole read load falls on the same instance, which becomes the scaling limit of the entire system.

finding.MISSING_CACHE.direct.message.one: '{node}' takes direct queries from {count} component with no cache and no read replica.
finding.MISSING_CACHE.direct.message.other: '{node}' takes direct queries from {count} components with no cache and no read replica.

finding.MISSING_CACHE.direct.suggestion: Place a cache in front of the most frequent reads, or configure read replicas on the database.
finding.MISSING_CACHE.passed.explanation: Each database's callers were checked: none receives enough direct load to become the system's scaling limit.
finding.MISSING_CACHE.passed.message: Database access is backed by a cache or by replicas.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.exposedToSpof: Since '{target}' is a single point of failure, its outage propagates directly back to the caller.
Add a circuit breaker or an alternative response for when the destination does not reply.
Add a circuit breaker so the call fails fast when the destination does not reply: a write has no meaningful alternative response. And if the operation can wait, place a queue in between.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.noTimeout.exp: Without a timeout, a slow response holds on to resources indefinitely.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.noTimeout.sug: Configure a timeout appropriate to the operation.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.noTimeoutAndS: Without a timeout, a slow response holds on to resources indefinitely — and since '{target}' is a single point of failure, its outage propagates directly back to the caller.
Configure a timeout appropriate to the operation, and add a circuit breaker or an alternative response for when the destination does not reply.

Configure a timeout appropriate to the operation and add a circuit breaker so the call fails fast when the destination does not reply: a write has no meaningful alternative response. And if the operation can wait, place a queue in between.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.passed.explan: Every synchronous call has a timeout bounding it and, where the destination is critical, an alternative to fall back on if it does not respond.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.passed.messag: The synchronous calls are protected against failure.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.telemetryPush: Sending telemetry synchronously with no timeout places '{target}' on the request path: if the metrics collector slows down or goes down, the request waits with it.
Make the send asynchronous: telemetry is fire-and-forget, and a call that does not wait for a response cannot hold the request up. If it must be synchronous, give it at least a timeout.
finding.MISSING_RESILIENCE.unprotected.m: The call from '{source}' to '{target}' has no protection against failure.
finding.NO_OBSERVABILITY.blind.explanati: There is not a single connection to observability in the whole diagram, so when something fails nobody will know what failed, since when, or what caused it. This finding covers the whole system and is charged only once: as soon as the first component is wired, this critical becomes one warning per component still unwired, and the area's score improves with each connection.
finding.NO_OBSERVABILITY.blind.message: The system is blind: none of its {count:number} components is observed.
finding.NO_OBSERVABILITY.blind.suggestio: Add an observability component and wire the components to it one by one, starting with the entry point and the system of record: those are the first two to inspect when something goes wrong.

'{telemetry}' already exists, but nothing reaches it: wire the components to it one by one, starting with the entry point and the system of record. An observability component with no incoming connection observes nothing.
There is already observability in the diagram, but nothing reaches it: wire the components to it one by one, starting with the entry point and the system of record.
finding.NO_OBSERVABILITY.passed.explanat: Every component of the system is connected to observability, so when something fails there will be a place to look — and it will indicate which component failed.
finding.NO_OBSERVABILITY.unobserved.expl: When '{node}' fails there will be nowhere to look: no record of how long it was taking, how many requests it lost, or whether it started the incident. Observability is not a component that is added; it is one connection per component, and this one has none.
finding.NO_OBSERVABILITY.unobserved.sugg: Add an observability component and wire '{node}' to it, along with everything else worth inspecting when something goes wrong.
Wire '{node}' to '{telemetry}'. Either direction: the component pushing or the observability scraping it, both count.
Wire '{node}' to one of the observability components already present.
finding.NO_RATE_LIMIT.passed.explanation: The entry point rejects at the door whatever exceeds the limit, instead of letting it pile up on the components behind it.
finding.NO_RATE_LIMIT.passed.message: The entry point caps how many requests it accepts.
finding.NO_RATE_LIMIT.unlimited.explanat: Every arriving request is admitted, so a spike — or a deliberate attack — propagates all the way inside, and the most fragile component pays the price.
finding.NO_RATE_LIMIT.unlimited.message: '{node}' does not limit the requests it accepts.
finding.NO_RATE_LIMIT.unlimited.suggesti: Set a request limit consistent with what the components behind it can withstand: the excess is rejected at the entry point, where rejection is cheap.

Set a request limit on the API consistent with what sits behind it, or place a gateway in front that does it on its behalf: whatever exceeds the limit is rejected at the entry point, where rejection is cheap.

A service does not limit requests; the entry point in front of it does. Place a gateway between the client and the service with a limit matched to what sits behind it — whatever exceeds it is rejected there, where rejection is cheap.
finding.ORPHAN_NODE.disconnected.explana: It neither receives calls nor makes any, so it is not part of any flow in the architecture.
finding.ORPHAN_NODE.disconnected.suggest: Wire it to whatever should call it or to whatever it should call, or delete it if it is no longer needed.
finding.ORPHAN_NODE.passed.explanation: A component with no incoming and no outgoing calls takes part in no flow, so no other rule can say anything about it.
finding.ORPHAN_NODE.passed.message: Every component is connected to something.
finding.OVERPROVISIONED.explanation: It receives {loadRps:number} rps, and {keep:number} copies would handle the same load with the same headroom. The {spare:number} extra copies account for {waste:number} of the {cost:number} units this component costs: capacity that is paid for and not used.
finding.OVERPROVISIONED.message: '{node}' has {copies:number} copies and uses {utilization:percent} of the capacity paid for.
finding.OVERPROVISIONED.passed.explanati: No component has spare copies for the declared load. What you pay extra for redundancy stops at the second copy, which is the one that takes it out of being a single point of failure.
finding.OVERPROVISIONED.passed.message: No capacity is being paid for without being used.
finding.OVERPROVISIONED.suggestion.datab: Remove replicas: the ones that answer no queries cost exactly as much as the ones that do. Keep as many as the load requires, plus one to cover an outage.
finding.OVERPROVISIONED.suggestion.insta: Reduce its instances to the smallest number that handles the declared load with headroom, and never below two: the second instance is not capacity — it is what removes the single point of failure.
finding.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.backwards.expl: Messages go in and never come out. '{worker}' points at '{node}', and in this model an arrow into a queue means publishing to it: the consumer receives the arrow from the queue. As drawn, '{worker}' is a second producer and nothing processes the messages.
finding.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.backwards.sugg: Reverse the arrow between '{worker}' and '{node}': the queue delivers to the worker, not the other way round.
Reverse the arrow between '{worker}' and '{node}': the topic delivers to its subscribers, not the other way round.
finding.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.passed.explana: Every queue and every topic somebody publishes to delivers its messages to some component, so the work entrusted to them gets done.
finding.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.passed.message: Everything published has somebody receiving it.
finding.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.unconsumed.exp: Messages go in and never come out: no component processes them, so the request is answered but the work handed over is never done, and the queue only grows.
finding.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.unconsumed.sug: Connect the queue to the component that processes its messages — usually a worker — with an arrow leaving the queue: it is the queue that delivers the message.

Subscribe the interested components to the topic, with an arrow leaving the topic towards each subscriber: the topic is what delivers each copy. A fact published with nobody listening never happened as far as the rest of the system is concerned.
finding.QUEUE_NO_DLQ.missing.explanation: A message that cannot be processed is retried, fails again and disappears without a trace. Nobody finds out what was lost.
finding.QUEUE_NO_DLQ.missing.suggestion: Enable the dead letter queue so that whatever fails ends up somewhere it can be reviewed.
finding.QUEUE_NO_DLQ.passed.explanation: A message that keeps failing ends up in the dead letter queue instead of being lost, and there it can be reviewed.
finding.QUEUE_NO_DLQ.passed.message: The queues have a place for what cannot be processed.
finding.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.chain.messag: Retries multiply along the chain {walk}: up to {factor:number} requests for every original one.
finding.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.explanation: When a service starts failing, the retries at each hop multiply with one another and add load precisely on the component that is already struggling.
finding.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.passed.expla: Retries were multiplied along every synchronous chain, and none of them builds up into an avalanche of requests.
finding.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.passed.messa: The retries that are configured do not amplify along a chain.
finding.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.suggestion: Retry only at the hop closest to the failure, add growing waits between attempts, and cap retries on the intermediate segments.

finding.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.unbounded.me.one: The call from '{source}' to '{target}' retries {retries:number} time with no timeout to bound it.
finding.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.unbounded.me.other: The call from '{source}' to '{target}' retries {retries:number} times with no timeout to bound them.

finding.SHARED_DATABASE.passed.explanati: Every database and every object storage has at most one service using it, so each service can change its data without affecting the others.
finding.SHARED_DATABASE.passed.message: No store is shared by several services.
finding.SHARED_DATABASE.readers.explanat: Reading another service's schema also creates coupling, though of a different kind: the writer of '{node}' cannot change a table without breaking its readers, and each reader is tied to a data model it does not control. It is not integration through the database in its full form — no service overwrites another's data — which is why the advice is not to split the store but to stop reading it directly.

finding.SHARED_DATABASE.readers.message.one: '{node}' is read directly by {count} service: {names}, and the diagram declares that access as read-only.
finding.SHARED_DATABASE.readers.message.other: '{node}' is read directly by {count} services: {names}, and the diagram declares those accesses as read-only.

finding.SHARED_DATABASE.readers.suggesti: Let the owner of the data expose what the others need through its API, or publish events from which each reader can maintain its own read copy. If a reader needs half the schema, it is probably part of the same service.
finding.SHARED_DATABASE.shared.explanati: The services sharing '{node}' are not independent: the schema is the interface between them, and changing it for one means touching the others. Each deploys on its own, but none can evolve on its own. This is integration through the database, the kind of coupling that is hardest to undo later.

finding.SHARED_DATABASE.shared.message.one: '{node}' is the store shared by {count} service: {names}.
finding.SHARED_DATABASE.shared.message.other: '{node}' is the store shared by {count} services: {names}.

finding.SHARED_DATABASE.shared.suggestio: Give each service its own data, and let the others request it through its API or learn about changes through a queue. If two services need the same tables, they are probably the same service.
finding.SHARED_DATABASE.writers.explanat: Several services write to the same schema of '{node}', and this time the diagram declares it explicitly rather than it being inferred. This is integration through the database in its full form: each writer can break the others' data, and the schema is a contract nobody signed.
finding.SHARED_DATABASE.writers.suggesti: One schema, one owner: allow a single service to write, and have the rest request changes through its API or publish events. If two services need to write to the same tables, they are probably the same service.
finding.SPOF.explanation.covered: No request stops being served if '{node}' goes down: every caller reaches it asynchronously or has a fallback. What is lost is not requests but what lies behind them — the state it holds, or the work that never gets done — and that is not measured here.
finding.SPOF.explanation.measured: If '{node}' goes down, {affected:percent} of the requests coming in the front door stop being served. There is no equivalent component that could take over its work.
finding.SPOF.explanation.unmeasured: The impact cannot be measured: no request has a way in, because every component depends on some other one. What is certain is that whatever calls it synchronously and unprotected goes down with it, measured or not.
finding.SPOF.passed.explanation: Component by component, the analysis checked what would stop working if it went down: none of them takes several others down with it.
finding.SPOF.passed.message: No component has several others depending on it without redundancy.
finding.SPOF.sameZone.explanation: Redundancy answers two questions — how many copies exist and where they are — and only the first is answered here. The copies exist, but none is outside zone {zone}: those that declare a zone are in it, and those that declare none cannot be placed anywhere, which for an outage amounts to the same thing. An outage that takes the zone down can take all of them at once. This is evaluated as soon as one copy declares a zone; a diagram with no zones at all is not.

finding.SPOF.sameZone.message.one: {names} has all of its copies in zone {zone}: it survives losing a machine, but not losing the zone.
finding.SPOF.sameZone.message.other: {names} are the same component repeated, and of the {count} copies none is outside zone {zone}.

finding.SPOF.shared.message.one: '{node}' is a single point of failure: {count} component depends on it with no redundancy.
finding.SPOF.shared.message.other: '{node}' is a single point of failure: {count} components depend on it with no redundancy.

finding.SPOF.suggestion.cache: Spread it over several nodes — declare its instances — and give whoever queries it a fallback to the origin: a cache that cannot be lost has ceased to be a cache.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.database: Add replicas with automatic failover, and verify that promoting a new primary requires no human intervention. A read replica spreads load; it does not take over from the primary when it goes down.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.entryPoint: Declare a second instance for it, or draw two and place them behind a load balancer with a health check, in different zones. It is the entry point: while only one exists, everything behind it inherits its availability.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.external: It can neither be replicated nor fixed, so the decision is what to do without it: a fallback response, a second provider, or moving the operation out of the customer's request.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.identityProvider: It cannot be replicated, so the solution is not to depend on it on every request: validate the token's signature locally and cache it instead of calling the provider each time, and declare what a valid session does when the provider does not respond — continuing with the session it already has is a fallback, and it is the one that clears this finding.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.instances: Add a second equivalent instance behind a load balancer. It holds no state, so its consumers cannot tell which of the two responded.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.objectStorage: Enable its replication: it declares that every file lives in more than one place. Unlike a stateless component, another copy gains nothing here — what has to be replicated are the files — and that is why it is a switch and not a number.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.queue: Declare the broker's copies: with two or more instances the queue stops being a single machine. Outside the model, that corresponds to a cluster with the queue mirrored and persisted to disk — what cannot be lost are the messages already accepted. A dead consumer catches up on its own; a lost queue does not.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.sameZone: Keep at least one copy in another zone, and declare it: a copy with no declared zone does not count as being elsewhere. If redundancy is declared as an instance count, model the instances as separate components behind the balancer: it is the only way the diagram can state where each one runs. Distributing them does not change their number: two copies in two zones cost the same as two in one.
finding.SPOF.suggestion.topic: Declare the broker's copies: with two or more instances the topic stops being a single machine. Outside the model, that corresponds to a cluster with the topic replicated and split into partitions — a dead subscriber catches up on its own; a lost topic takes its history with it.

finding.SPOF.unreachable.message.one: '{node}' is a single point of failure: {count} component becomes unreachable if it stops working.
finding.SPOF.unreachable.message.other: '{node}' is a single point of failure: {count} components become unreachable if it stops working.

finding.SYNC_CHAIN.long.explanation: The request is not finished until the last link responds: the latencies add up, and one link failing is enough for all of them to fail. What counts are the components that run logic — APIs, services, workers and third parties; a CDN, a gateway, a load balancer, a cache or a store along the way is a layer the call crosses, not another link.

finding.SYNC_CHAIN.long.message.one: '{node}' starts a synchronous chain of {count} service.
finding.SYNC_CHAIN.long.message.other: '{node}' starts a synchronous chain of {count} services.

finding.SYNC_CHAIN.long.suggestion: Cut the chain by introducing a queue at the point where the operation stops needing an immediate response.
finding.SYNC_CHAIN.long.suggestion.read: A queue cuts nothing here: the request is waiting for the data at the end, and a read cannot be deferred. Shorten the path instead of splitting it: let the component that responds read directly — from a cache, or from a replica fed asynchronously — or merge the intermediate services if all they do is pass the question along. If this chain is a write, declare it on the last edge and the solution becomes a queue again.
finding.SYNC_CHAIN.passed.explanation: The synchronous calls were traversed and none chains enough services for the latencies to accumulate.
finding.SYNC_CHAIN.passed.message: There are no long synchronous chains.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT.expires.explan: The call takes {callMs:durationPrecise} with everything working, and the timeout is {timeoutMs:durationPrecise}: it expires every time, so '{target}' behaves as if it were permanently down.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT.expires.messag: The timeout on the call from '{source}' to '{target}' is shorter than the call itself.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT.expires.sugges: Before modifying the number, look at the capacity: the call takes {callMs:durationPrecise} because there is a queue in front of '{target}', not because the operation is long. Raising the timeout only produces a slower response — what makes the call fit is more capacity behind it, or less work per request. A circuit breaker will make it fail sooner, but it will not make it fit either.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT.passed.explana: Every timeout is longer than what its call takes with everything working, so it only fires when something is genuinely wrong.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT.passed.message: The timeouts give each call time to finish.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.passed.explanat: Every timeout sits below what the model treats as an unbounded wait, so when the far end hangs, the call fails in time for something to be done about it.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.passed.message: The timeouts are limits, not waits.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.unbounded.expla: The call takes {callMs:durationPrecise} with everything working, and a call with no timeout is abandoned by the model at {waitMs:duration}. A timeout of {timeoutMs:duration} offers exactly as much protection as none: if '{target}' hangs, the caller waits as long as it would have waited with no limit at all, and until the timeout expires no other mechanism on the call — retries, circuit breaker, alternative response — can act.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.unbounded.messa: The timeout on the call from '{source}' to '{target}' is {timeoutMs:duration}: that is a wait, not a limit.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.unbounded.sugge: Lower it to a few times what the call takes ({callMs:durationPrecise}): high enough that a spike does not trip it, and short enough that a hung far end turns into an error somebody can handle.
finding.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.unboundedToSpof: The call takes {callMs:durationPrecise} with everything working, and a call with no timeout is abandoned by the model at {waitMs:duration}. A timeout of {timeoutMs:duration} offers exactly as much protection as none — and since '{target}' is a single point of failure with nothing covering this call, that wait applies to every request going through it: its outage does not become an error, it becomes a queue of waiting users.
finding.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.passed.message: The entry points' limits admit the arriving traffic.
finding.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.passed.explanat: The traffic arriving at each entry point was compared with its rate limit: none is rejecting a substantial share of its declared traffic.
finding.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.shedding.messag: '{node}' rejects {rejected:percent} of the traffic that reaches it.
finding.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.shedding.explan: {demandRps:number} requests per second arrive at '{node}' and its limit admits {admittedRps:number}. Limiting is not scaling: the limit protects what is behind it, but those users are not served by anyone — and since rejected traffic never touches the system, everything inside appears healthy.
finding.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.shedding.sugges: Determine which of the two figures is incorrect. If the declared traffic is real, add capacity behind the limit and raise it; if the limit is right, the traffic declaration is inflated. The notice disappears when the two figures are consistent.
finding.MISSING_CDN.passed.message: The heavy traffic enters through the edge.
finding.MISSING_CDN.passed.explanation: The high-traffic entry points have a CDN in front, so the edge absorbs its share before requests touch the system.
finding.MISSING_CDN.direct.message: '{node}' serves {loadRps:number} requests per second with no CDN in front.
finding.MISSING_CDN.direct.explanation: Everything that reaches '{node}' is served by your infrastructure, request by request. A CDN would absorb its hit ratio of that traffic at the edge — the cheapest form of scaling, because what it absorbs never even arrives.
finding.MISSING_CDN.direct.suggestion: Place a CDN between the outside and the entry point. If the traffic is purely dynamic and there is nothing to cache at the edge, leave the diagram as it is: this notice raises a question; it does not assert an error.
finding.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.contradict: Two explicit declarations contradict each other: the configuration of '{node}' states that it does not require authentication, while the diagram wires it to '{provider}', which declares that it does. The analysis will not decide which of the two is true.
'{node}' declares no authentication and is wired to '{provider}'.
A decision is required: enable authentication on '{node}' if it really delegates to '{provider}', or remove the arrow if it does not.
finding.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.open.expla: It is an entry point from outside with data behind it, so anyone who knows the address can reach it.
finding.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.open.sugge: Enable authentication on the entry point, or place a gateway in front that provides it.
finding.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.passed.exp: Anyone arriving from outside must identify themselves before the request reaches anything that stores data.
finding.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.undeclared: It is an entry point from outside, traffic reaches it, and there is data behind it. Nothing declares whether identification is required to reach it, and an entry point nobody has vouched for is considered open until proven otherwise: it weighs the same as one that explicitly requires no authentication.
'{node}' does not declare whether it requires authentication.

Declare the entry point's authentication. If it has authentication, declaring it closes this finding; if it does not, declaring it changes nothing in the weight — it already counts as open — but makes clear what has to be corrected first.
Outside traffic reaches '{node}' without passing through anything that could verify who is calling. It is not an API, a gateway or a service: it has no way to request identification, and nothing in front of it does so on its behalf.
The outside reaches '{node}' with no entry point in front.
Place an entry point in front — an API or a gateway — and allow only that component to talk to '{node}'. If it is genuinely internal and receives no outside traffic, remove the arrow that reaches it.
It receives {loadRps:number} rps and handles {capacityRps:number}, {utilization:percent} of its capacity. Any spike above the declared load will overwhelm it.

It receives {loadRps:number} writes per second, and the primary with its replicas handles {capacityRps:number}, {utilization:percent}: read replicas do not absorb writes. Any peak above the declared load will overwhelm it.
'{node}' is at the edge of its capacity.
It receives {loadRps:number} rps and handles {capacityRps:number}, {utilization:percent} of its capacity. What does not fit fails, and what does fit waits longer.

It receives {loadRps:number} rps and handles {capacityRps:number}, {utilization:percent} of its capacity. What does not fit fails and what does fit waits longer, but saturating is not the same as rejecting at the door: the components behind it keep receiving the traffic all the same.

It receives {loadRps:number} writes per second, and the primary with its replicas handles {capacityRps:number}, {utilization:percent}: read replicas do not absorb writes. What does not fit fails, and what does fit waits longer.
'{node}' receives more requests than it can handle.
finding.UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT.passed.expl: Every component handles what reaches it with room to spare, so a spike will not overwhelm it.
finding.UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT.passed.mess: No component is near its capacity under the declared load.
Place a cache in front so that not everything reaches it, add read replicas, or move the work that can wait out of the request.
A bucket is not sized: take work off it. Place a CDN in front of whatever is served as-is, or reduce the files per request — the replication that can be declared buys redundancy, not capacity.
Read replicas do not absorb writes: add full replicas, or move the writes that can wait out of the request and place a queue in front of them.
Add consumers: the queue itself can cope; it is the consumer that cannot keep up.
Give it more instances, or split its work across several components.

rule.na.ASYNC_NO_QUEUE.noAsyncCall: No call is asynchronous. This rule watches fire-and-forget work: mark a call as asynchronous and it will ask where the work waits.
rule.na.CACHE_AS_STORE.noCache: No cache is called from inside the system. As soon as one of the components reads from or writes to one, this rule will check whether that data lives anywhere else.
rule.na.CYCLE.noCalls: There is no call between the components — instrumentation does not count. A cycle needs at least one path that comes back on itself.
rule.na.EXPOSED_DATABASE.noStore: There is no data store wired into the flow. With no database and no object storage in it, there is nothing that could be left within anyone's reach.
rule.na.EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK.noExternalC: There is no call to a third-party service. Draw the provider and the call, and this rule will ask what happens the day it does not respond.
rule.na.HIGH_COUPLING.noCalls: No component calls another one yet. Coupling is counted on the arrows leaving each component, and none leaves yet.
rule.na.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.noCalls: There is no call between the components — instrumentation does not count. This rule reads the direction of each arrow, and none points anywhere yet.
rule.na.MISSING_CACHE.noDatabase: No database is queried by anything. Wire up its readers and this rule will check whether those reads call for a cache or a read replica.
rule.na.MISSING_CDN.lowTraffic: No entry point reaches {traffic:number} requests per second. Below that threshold a CDN is an optimisation, not a decision that changes the design.
rule.na.MISSING_CDN.noLoad: No load has been declared. Without requests per second there is no way to tell whether the edge would take work off the infrastructure.
rule.na.MISSING_RESILIENCE.noSyncCall: No call is synchronous. Only a caller that waits for a response can be left waiting: draw one and this rule will ask about its timeout and its fallback.
rule.na.NO_OBSERVABILITY.nothingToWatch: No component is wired into the flow to be observed. Coverage is measured over what takes part in the flow, not over disconnected components.
rule.na.NO_OBSERVABILITY.singleComponent: There is no more than one component on the canvas. Requiring telemetry of a single-component sketch would be noise.
rule.na.NO_RATE_LIMIT.noTrafficAtDoor: No public-facing entry point receives any declared traffic. A limit only means something once there is a wired entry point with requests per second.
rule.na.ORPHAN_NODE.singleComponent: There is no more than one component on the canvas. With a single component — or with none — there is nothing to be disconnected from.
rule.na.OVERPROVISIONED.noLoad: No load has been declared. With no traffic there is no way to tell what capacity is spare: declare the requests per second at the origin and this rule will indicate which copies are being paid for unnecessarily.
rule.na.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.noQueue: There is no queue and no topic wired to anything. Draw one and this rule will check whether anything picks up what gets published.
rule.na.QUEUE_NO_DLQ.noQueue: There is no queue wired to anything. Draw one between the component that publishes and the one that processes, and this rule will ask where the messages that cannot be processed end up.
rule.na.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.noRetries: No call declares retries. With no retry count on the arrows there is nothing to multiply downstream.
rule.na.SHARED_DATABASE.noStore: No data store receives any call — no database, no object storage. Wire the component that uses it and this rule will check how many services the schema belongs to.
rule.na.SPOF.noDependency: No component depends on another one yet. Wire two components together and this rule will check what each one takes down with it.
rule.na.SYNC_CHAIN.noSyncCall: No call is synchronous. A chain is measured by stacking waits, and there is no wait yet.
rule.na.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.noTimeout: No call declares a timeout. Declare one and this rule will state whether it is a real limit or merely a long wait.
rule.na.TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT.noTimeout: No call declares a timeout. Declare one on the arrow and this rule will compare it with what the destination actually takes.
rule.na.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.noLimit: No component declares a request limit. With no limit nothing is rejected: the excess is admitted anyway, and what happens next is covered by UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT.
rule.na.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.noLoad: No traffic has been declared. With no requests per second at the origin there is nothing that could be rejected by a limit.
rule.na.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.nothingExp: Nothing from outside reaches the system's data, and nothing from outside comes in through a component that is not an entry point. Wire the entry point to whatever holds the information and this rule will ask who authenticates.
rule.na.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.noTrafficA: There is an entry point with data behind it, but nothing calls it yet: no declared traffic reaches it and no Client is drawn. Declare the traffic that comes in through it — or draw its caller — and this rule will ask whether it authenticates.
rule.na.UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT.noLoad: No load has been declared. Declare the requests per second on whatever originates the traffic and this rule will indicate which component falls short.
sim.edge.contained: '{target}' does not respond and the alternative response is served.
sim.edge.breakerOpen: '{target}' responds worse and the circuit breaker stops calling it.
sim.edge.injected: A fault was injected into this call: the destination is still alive, but it cannot be reached.
sim.edge.instanceDown: The instance it routes to is not answering.
sim.edge.noTimeout: '{target}' does not respond and the call has no timeout: it waits {waitMs:duration} without giving up.
sim.edge.timeoutExceeded: It takes {callMs:duration} against a {timeoutMs:duration} timeout: it expires every time.
sim.edge.unprotected: '{target}' does not respond and the call has no alternative.
sim.edge.unreachable: It never occurs: its originator receives no traffic from '{cause}'.
sim.node.contained: '{target}' does not respond, but the alternative response keeps the service up. It still works, with reduced functionality.
sim.node.degradedDependency: '{target}' responds worse, and its call propagates the degradation.
sim.node.breakerOpen: '{target}' responds worse, and the circuit breaker cuts that call instead of waiting for it: the slowness stays there and does not climb. It still works, with reduced functionality.
sim.node.injected: A fault was injected into this component.
sim.node.instanceDown.contained: One of its instances is not answering; the health check routes traffic to the rest.
sim.node.instanceDown.spreading: One of its instances is not answering and it still receives traffic: with no health check, the degradation does not stop here.
sim.node.noTimeout: Its call to '{target}' has no timeout: it waits indefinitely, and neither the retry nor the fallback gets to run.
sim.node.noWork: No work reaches it because the queue is unavailable.
sim.node.overloaded: It receives {loadRps:number} rps and handles {capacityRps:number}: it serves {served:number} out of every 100 requests and rejects the rest.
sim.node.queueDown: The work is not enqueued, but it keeps serving requests.
sim.node.saturated: It is at {utilization:percent} of its capacity: it receives {loadRps:number} rps and handles {capacityRps:number}. Any spike will overwhelm it.
sim.node.timeoutExceeded: The call to '{target}' takes {callMs:duration} and the timeout is {timeoutMs:duration}: it expires every time, as if '{target}' were down.
sim.node.unprotected: Its call to '{target}' has no alternative when '{target}' does not respond.
sim.node.unreachable: No traffic reaches it: '{cause}' was its entry path.

ui.fault.degraded.detail: It responds more slowly and propagates the degradation upstream, unless the call has a circuit breaker.
ui.fault.down.edge: A partition: the component is still running, but out of reach.
ui.fault.latency.detail: It changes nothing until a timeout is exceeded.
ui.field.access.effect: The invisible field: no search finds it by name, yet three rules and the model all read it. Marking the call as write-only removes it from the reads MISSING_CACHE counts, and several declared writers change the message SHARED_DATABASE reports. A declared write carries real weight: read replicas do not absorb it (UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT), its fallback neither counts as a served request nor discounts the single point of failure, and a declared read that does not wait for the data is a critical finding about the diagram (IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY). A fallback on a write is likewise a warning about the diagram (IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY): on a write, the MISSING_RESILIENCE button offers a timeout and a circuit breaker, and MISSING_CACHE's automatic fix only reroutes reads — a call that also writes stays on the database and requires no cache.
ui.field.authentication.effect: Together with a declared call to an identity provider, it is the only thing standing between a guarded entry point and a critical UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY. Declaring it as “no” with an identity provider behind it is the contradiction the rule reports explicitly.
ui.field.circuitBreaker.effect: It cuts the failure off instead of letting it climb: the call fails immediately, does not wait for the timeout, and stops multiplying the retries. It is one of the three ways to resolve MISSING_RESILIENCE.
ui.field.deadLetterQueue.effect: It is the only defence against silent loss: a message the queue cannot deliver ends up somewhere instead of vanishing. It is also the only thing that resolves QUEUE_NO_DLQ.
ui.field.fallback.effect: It contains the failure: the caller ends up degraded rather than down. With a timeout declared, the request is still served, which is why it also reduces what is lost when the target goes down.
ui.field.healthCheck.effect: Without it, the balancer keeps sending traffic to a downed instance and the failure reaches the entry point; with it, the failure stays contained in the lost instance. An architecture can withstand a fault better without scoring better, and nowhere is that clearer than here.
ui.field.hitRatio.effect: What the cache answers never travels on. Undeclared, the model assumes 0.8 on a Cache and 0.9 on a CDN; set to 1, nothing reaches what is behind it and the model stops seeing it entirely.
ui.field.hitRatio.formula: load that goes on = load × (1 − hitRatio)
ui.field.instances.effect: It multiplies the component's capacity, so it is what keeps UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT away. With two or more declared, the component also stops being a single point of failure.
ui.field.jobsPerSecond.effect: This is the load the scheduler introduces into the system, exactly like the requests per second of a root. No rule reads it by name, yet everything that depends on load moves with it.
ui.field.jobsPerSecond.formula: utilization ρ = load / capacity · queueing = min( 1 / (1 − ρ) , 20 )
ui.field.maxRetries.effect: It only matters when the consumer is not healthy: then the queue redelivers and the cost of that call is multiplied. Under normal operation it has no effect.
ui.field.maxRetries.formula: cost = cost × (maxRetries + 1), only with the consumer affected
ui.field.rateLimit.effect: It trims the admitted load at the entry point: whatever exceeds the limit is rejected and never reaches what is behind it. It flattens the traffic curve and, in exchange, drops requests.
ui.field.readReplicas.effect: It adds capacity the way replicas do and, in addition, resolves MISSING_CACHE: with a single read replica the model considers that database's reads already spread.
ui.field.readReplicas.formula: capacity = one instance's capacity × (1 + replicas + read replicas)
ui.field.reads.both: The simulator and the rules both read it.
ui.field.reads.load: The simulator reads it, and the capacity rules through the load.
ui.field.reads.nobody: Nothing reads it: neither the simulator nor a single rule.
ui.field.reads.rules: Only the rules read it: it does not change the simulation.
ui.field.reads.simulation: Only the simulator reads it: it does not alter the score.
ui.field.replicas.effect: Each replica adds one more instance's worth of capacity, and with a single one declared the database stops being a single point of failure.
ui.field.replicas.formula: capacity = one instance's capacity × (1 + replicas + read replicas)
ui.field.replicated.effect: It declares that every file lives in more than one place, which is the only thing that removes the bucket from being a single point of failure: it is the equivalent of a database's replicas. It adds no capacity — a saturated bucket is not fixed with more copies — and changes nothing in the simulation.
ui.field.requestsPerSecond.effect: This is the load that enters here. Every component's utilization, the queueing factor that multiplies the latencies, and every capacity rule derive from it.
ui.field.requestsPerSecond.formula: utilization ρ = load / capacity · queueing = min( 1 / (1 − ρ) , 20 )
ui.field.retries.effect: It multiplies the load this call imposes on its target, and the worse the target is doing, the more it multiplies. It only counts if the call has a declared timeout: without one, the model amplifies nothing.
ui.field.retries.formula: load = load × (1 + retries × (1 − the target's yield))
ui.field.timeoutSeconds.effect: It is the call's limit: if the call takes longer, the hop expires. It is also the key to the retries — with no declared timeout the model amplifies no load, however many retries are set.
ui.field.timeoutSeconds.formula: if the hop's latency > timeout → the hop expires
ui.field.type.effect: It is documentation: the engine entered travels in the file and appears in the export, but nothing in the analysis reads it. Choosing Postgres over Mongo alters no figure.

ui.term.synchronous.definition: The caller waits for the response before continuing, so its latency adds to the request's and its failure is the request's failure. The analysis is guided by this checkbox and never by the protocol: fire-and-forget over HTTP and a call that waits over a queue are both real. Unticking it removes failure propagation; it does not provide durability: between two working components, a call that does not wait needs a queue in between where the work can wait (ASYNC_NO_QUEUE).
ui.term.timeout.definition: How long the caller is willing to wait before giving the call up for lost. With no timeout a slow response holds resources indefinitely, and the model does not give up until 30 s. It bounds the wait; it does not obtain a response.
ui.term.retries.definition: How many times the call is repeated when it fails. Retries multiply across hops: two retries over two links are nine calls against the far end, and they arrive exactly when it was already in difficulty (RETRY_AMPLIFICATION). With no timeout they never happen: a retry requires the first call to be given up on.
ui.term.circuitBreaker.definition: After a series of failures it stops trying and fails immediately, instead of waiting out the timeout. It stops insisting on something that is already down and returns control at once; but what it returns is still a failure, only a cheap one.
ui.term.fallback.definition: A response that can be served when the real one does not arrive: the last known value, a default, a reduced version. It cuts the failure off on its way back: a timeout bounds the wait, but when it fires there is still no response (EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK). What it does not stop is slowness: while the target responds within the timeout the caller keeps waiting for it, and that is what the circuit breaker is for.
ui.term.entryPoint.definition: A component that nothing inside the diagram calls: that is where traffic comes in. It is the only place where declaring requests per second means anything, and it is the point Security asks whether identity is required; behind an entry point, that question is already answered.
ui.term.deadLetterQueue.definition: The place where a message ends up when the queue could not deliver it after its retries. Without one, that message is retried, fails again and disappears without a trace: nobody learns what was lost (QUEUE_NO_DLQ).
ui.term.hitRatio.definition: The share of reads the cache answers on its own. What it hits never reaches the origin, so it is literally the load the database never sees. A CDN starts from a higher ratio than a cache: static content is the most cacheable traffic there is.
ui.term.rateLimit.definition: The ceiling on what an entry point admits. It protects what is behind it from a spike — or from a deliberate attack — but limiting is not scaling: what does not get in is served by nobody, and those users are counted (TRAFFIC_REJECTED).
ui.term.readReplicas.definition: Copies of the database that only serve reads. They add read capacity without touching writes, which still go to a single machine — which is why they spread the load and do not, on their own, remove the single point of failure.
ui.term.instances.definition: How many copies of the component run at once. The model's capacity is per copy, so this is what multiplies it — and it is also the shortcut a challenge may forbid, because scaling out is not always the lesson.
ui.term.loadAmplification.definition: How much one incoming request is multiplied inside the system. Every synchronous call that fans out, every retry and every copy a topic hands out counts: one user request can become ten against the component at the far end.
ui.term.partition.definition: A call cut with both ends alive: neither has gone down, they simply can no longer reach each other. It is what a fault placed on an arrow injects, and it resembles an outage only from the calling side.

ui.impact.cascade.arithmetic:
cost(node) = processing(type) + max over synchronous edges of cost(edge)

cost(edge) =
    target healthy      hop(protocol) + cost(target) + injected latency
    over the timeout    timeout × (retries + 1)      ← and the target counts as down
    target down
      circuit breaker   ~0
      with timeout      timeout × (retries + 1)
      without timeout   30 s  (UnboundedWait)
    asynchronous        0
ui.impact.cascade.budget.over: The budget is exceeded by {value:number} ms.
ui.impact.cascade.budget.under: Inside the budget, with {value:number} ms to spare.
ui.impact.cascade.expired: The call expires every time: it is charged its timeout, not the hop plus the subtree.
ui.impact.cascade.failedCall: A failed call costs its timeout, not the hop plus the subtree: the work after it never happens. That is half the reason a short timeout is cheaper than a long one.
ui.impact.cascade.legend: Each bar starts where the one above it ended, and its parts add up to exactly what it measures. Where there are branches, the path keeps the slowest one and never the sum: that is why adding a dependency faster than the existing one does not appear here.
ui.impact.cascade.offScale: It exceeds the scale, which reaches {value:number} ms. A wait is not work, and it does not set the chart's scale.
ui.impact.cascade.raw: Had it been allowed to finish, it would have taken {value:duration}.
ui.impact.cascade.segment.injected.why: the latency added by hand at this step: the call's plus the component's.
ui.impact.cascade.segment.network.why: the protocol hop, the one figure that depends on how the call travels rather than on who answers it.
ui.impact.cascade.segment.processing.why: what the component takes at rest: the figure the model publishes for its type, applied to a component of the diagram.
ui.impact.cascade.segment.queueing.why: what it adds for being full: its processing under the queueing factor, minus its processing at rest. Today this only ever reads as a consequence inside a finding.
ui.impact.cascade.title: Where the latency goes
ui.impact.cascade.twoNumbers: A timeout is resolved by comparing two numbers, without simulating a single second, and that yields the cascading-timeout lesson at no cost: whoever calls something that expires sees a cost large enough to exceed their own timeout.
ui.impact.cascade.unbounded: No timeout: the call is abandoned at {value:duration}, and neither the retry nor the fallback gets to run.
ui.impact.cascade.unreachable: The target does not respond: the call is charged its timeout.
ui.impact.empty: Select a component or a call on the canvas and induce its failure to observe the result.
ui.impact.formula.amplification: Π(retries + 1) along the worst synchronous path = ×{value:amount}
ui.impact.formula.amplification.why: only failing calls with a timeout multiply: with no timeout the retry never happens, and a circuit breaker cuts it at the root.
ui.impact.formula.backlog: Σ (what reaches the queue − what its consumer absorbs) = +{value:amount} rps
ui.impact.formula.backlog.why: a rate, not a quantity: stating that it grows requires no time reference.
ui.impact.formula.blastRadius.why: everything down plus everything degraded, over every component.
ui.impact.formula.bottleneck: min(capacity / load) along the call tree = {name}
ui.impact.formula.bottleneck.why: whatever set that minimum. A component over its capacity is not down: it serves what it can and rejects the rest.
ui.impact.formula.componentsDegraded.why: the ones still answering, but worse: inherited degradation, work that no longer reaches them, or load above 80% of their capacity.
ui.impact.formula.componentsDown.why: the ones that no longer respond: the injected fault, whatever depended on it through a synchronous call with nothing to contain the failure, and whatever was left with no route in.
ui.impact.formula.entryPoints.why: the entry points that do not end up healthy, over all of them. Degraded counts: it is serving worse, and calling that unaffected would amount to saying nothing happens to the user.
ui.impact.formula.latency: max(processing + slowest call) from every entry point
ui.impact.formula.latency.why: parallel branches keep the slowest one, not the sum. The two figures travel whole and never as their difference: failing fast can turn out faster than working.
ui.impact.formula.legend: None of these figures is out of 100: they are components, milliseconds and factors. Where there are branches, latency and amplification keep the worst one and never add them up; and requests lost is a bound that can be redone by hand, not a probability.
ui.impact.formula.loadAmplification: load on the busiest component / rps coming in the front door = ×{value:amount}
ui.impact.formula.loadAmplification.why: a router splits and a fan-out adds. That is why breaking a monolith into three relieves nothing, and drawing a second gateway does not double what reaches the database.
ui.impact.formula.requestsAffected.why: what the worst entry point stops serving. It is the minimum along the call tree, not the product of its branches: two components at 50% in series give 50%, not 25%.

ui.legend.containedNote: An amber ring and, inside the component, the name of the mechanism that stopped the cascade. It marks the difference between three components down and seven.
ui.legend.degradedNote: Amber. Still in service, but responding worse, and that degradation propagates upstream.
ui.legend.downNote: Red. It has stopped responding, and the call reaching it is drawn dashed.
ui.legend.flowNote: The busiest call in the diagram is drawn in stronger ink; the thickness never changes. The exact figure for each call appears on hover. With no declared traffic, or with all calls equal, they are all drawn alike.
ui.legend.healthyNote: No colour: healthy components are not decorated.
ui.legend.highlightedNote: An amber ring around the components and calls of the finding open in the panel.
ui.legend.load: The bar along the bottom edge
ui.legend.loadNote: The proportion of its capacity the component uses under the declared load. The notch marks {value:percent}, the point at which the analysis begins to warn: amber from there, red beyond capacity.
ui.legend.open: What each element on the canvas means
ui.legend.syncNote: A solid line. It propagates failure backwards: if the far end goes down, the caller is affected.
ui.legend.title: Legend
ui.legend.unsizedNote: They cannot be sized from the diagram — the users, a provider's edge, a third party's service, the identity provider, a clock and the telemetry sink — so a meter there would be a permanently empty gauge.
ui.legend.zoneDownNote: The frame turns red when everything it contains is down. This is what the failure of an entire zone looks like, as opposed to that of a single component: the fault affects everything sharing the location at once.
ui.legend.zoneNote: A dotted frame around everything that declares the same zone, with its letter in the corner. The zone is set in each component's inspector, and components that are not placed manually never carry one.
ui.lens.allNote: The whole diagram, with all seven questions at once.
