ui.mechanisms.headline: Eleven mechanisms, and what the model does with each one
ui.mechanisms.lead: There is a screen for the model, one for the rules and one for the diagram. This one covers the mechanisms: what each one solves, which figure it moves — with the formula in plain sight — and the one thing the analyser cannot state: when not to use it. It is the only one of the four that can be read before drawing anything.
ui.mechanisms.whyNot: All eleven sheets share the same five bands, and the one that matters most is the fourth. The product knows how to penalise a missing mechanism but cannot teach what a mechanism costs: that is why payments-friday asks for timeouts while retry-storm shows retries bringing the system down. Both lessons are true, and knowing which one applies is the difference between passing challenges and understanding architecture.
ui.mechanisms.group.call.lead: Four settings on the same arrow, and the order matters: with no declared timeout, neither the retries nor the fallback is ever considered.
ui.mechanisms.group.between.lead: What breaks the synchronous chain, and what catches whatever fails along the way.
ui.mechanisms.group.load.lead: Three ways to send a component less load, or to make it withstand more. Inside the model they are nearly interchangeable; outside it, they are not.
ui.mechanisms.group.door.lead: Two settings on a single component that decide what gets in and where it is sent.
ui.mechanisms.band.model: What the model does with it
ui.mechanisms.noRules: No rule evaluates it: the score is the same with it and without it.
ui.mechanisms.tryLead: Opens a separate canvas, with three components and the mechanism switched off.
ui.mechanisms.tryFailed: The canvas could not be opened.
ui.mechanisms.closing: Reading a sheet modifies nothing of your own: all eleven are read-only. “Try it” does create a new canvas, with three components and the mechanism switched off, and adds it to your saved work like any other architecture. The same diagrams, without surrounding text, are on the proof sheet; the figures behind these formulas are on the model page.
ui.mechanism.timeout.problem: A call that never returns holds on to its caller. The timeout puts a ceiling on that wait and turns “still nothing” into a failure with a time attached.
ui.mechanism.timeout.model: A call costs the network hop, plus the target's own processing, plus the worst call the target makes in turn. If that total exceeds the ceiling, the hop comes out Expired and the response never arrives. With no declared timeout, a lost call does not cost what it takes: it costs the unbounded wait, a flat thirty seconds. It is also the key to the other two settings on the arrow — without it, neither the retries nor the fallback is ever considered (MISSING_RESILIENCE).
ui.mechanism.timeout.formula:
call = network + processing + worst hop below
call > timeout   →   Expired
failure with no timeout = 30,000 ms
failure with a timeout = timeout × (retries + 1)
ui.mechanism.timeout.avoid: Do not set it below what the call actually takes: a ceiling shorter than its own path always trips, and turns into a failure what was going to respond correctly (TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT). Do not use it to mask a saturated component: what is slow because of queueing stays slow, and all that changes is who gives up first; there the lesson is UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT. It also has a real ceiling of its own: from thirty seconds upwards it offers exactly as much protection as none at all (TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG).
ui.mechanism.retries.problem: Some failures do not repeat: a dropped packet, a restart, half a bad second. Repeating the call makes them disappear.
ui.mechanism.retries.model: This is the model's second non-linearity. Each retry multiplies the arrow's load by 1 + r × (1 − the target's yield): if the target answers everything, it costs nothing; if it is already struggling, it costs almost r times more — and it arrives at exactly the worst moment. When the call fails outright, the cost of the failure multiplies the same way. With no declared timeout the model does not count retries at all: repeating requires the first attempt to be given up on.
ui.mechanism.retries.formula:
arrow load × (1 + r × (1 − the target's yield))
cost of a failure = timeout × (r + 1)
no timeout: r does not count
ui.mechanism.retries.avoid: Do not direct them at something failing from saturation: the retry lands when the other end can no longer cope, and retries multiply across hops: two retries on two links are nine calls against the component at the bottom (RETRY_AMPLIFICATION). Nor at anything that is not repeatable: the model cannot tell a read from a charge, and charging twice is not a transient failure. If the goal is to stop insisting on something that is already down, the mechanism required is the circuit breaker.
ui.mechanism.circuitBreaker.problem: Once the other side is down, insisting only wastes time: every call waits out its whole timeout before being given up. The breaker stops trying and fails immediately.
ui.mechanism.circuitBreaker.model: Against an outage it does not contain the failure: the caller is left just as answerless, and what changes is the cost. With a breaker, a failed call costs 0 ms instead of timeout × (retries + 1), and amplification returns to 1 — in other words, it switches off the retries against something already down. Surviving an outage requires the other setting, the fallback. Against slowness, however, it is the only mechanism that helps: if the destination degrades, the breaker cuts that call instead of waiting for it, and the degradation does not climb: “Degrade” stops there.
ui.mechanism.circuitBreaker.formula:
down,  no breaker:  failure = timeout × (retries + 1)   ·   amplification = retries + 1
down,  breaker:     failure = 0 ms                      ·   amplification = 1
slow,  no breaker:  destination Degraded   →   caller Degraded (drags)
slow,  breaker:     destination Degraded   →   caller Degraded (contained)
ui.mechanism.circuitBreaker.avoid: Do not use it where the failure comes not from the other end but from your own load: opening the circuit adds no capacity, it only brings the rejection forward. And do not enable it expecting it to save the caller: what it returns is still a failure, only a cheap one. If the goal is not to go down with the other end, the setting is the fallback (EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK).
ui.mechanism.fallback.problem: A timeout bounds the wait, but when it fires there is still no response. The fallback is what can be served when the real answer does not arrive: the last known value, a default, a reduced version.
ui.mechanism.fallback.model: It is the mechanism on the arrow that cuts an outage off on its way back. With it, the caller comes out Degraded and contained instead of Down, and whatever sits behind it is never affected; the simulation names it explicitly when it happens. It requires a declared timeout: with no ceiling the model never reaches this setting, and the call drags the caller down anyway. What it does not stop is slowness: while the destination responds within the timeout the caller keeps calling, keeps waiting, and serves whatever arrives; that is what the circuit breaker is for.
ui.mechanism.fallback.formula:
no fallback:  destination Down       →   caller Down
fallback:     destination Down       →   caller Degraded (contained)
no timeout:   the box is not looked at
slowness:     destination Degraded   →   caller Degraded (the fallback does not stop it)
ui.mechanism.fallback.avoid: Do not enable it where there is nothing to respond with. The checkbox claims an alternative response exists, and the model believes it: if there is no default and no stale value worth serving behind it, an outage has been hidden inside the diagram, and the analysis will assign a score that has not been earned. On a write there is almost never an alternative: a payment that does not happen cannot be approximated.
ui.mechanism.queue.problem: In a synchronous chain, the last component decides the fate of the first. A queue in the middle breaks that: the work is recorded, and whoever performs it can be slow, or absent.
ui.mechanism.queue.model: An asynchronous call does not propagate the outage: the caller comes out Degraded and contained, and its latency cost is zero. What the consumer cannot absorb does not vanish — the queue delivers the smaller of what arrives and the consumer's capacity, and the rest accumulates as backlog, which the simulation counts separately from the score. The setting that decides all of this is “synchronous”, not the protocol.
ui.mechanism.queue.formula:
delivered = min(arriving, consumer capacity)
backlog += arriving − delivered
consumer Down   →   caller Degraded (contained)
ui.mechanism.queue.avoid: Do not use it when the caller needs the response immediately: a queue speeds nothing up, it trades “late” for “later”. If the long chain ends in a read, what needs shortening is the path — a cache or a replica — not a queue placed in front of it (SYNC_CHAIN). And a queue nothing consumes from is not asynchrony: it is a place where messages go in and never come out (QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER).
ui.mechanism.deadLetterQueue.problem: A message the queue cannot deliver is retried, fails again and disappears. Nobody learns what was lost. The dead letter queue is where it ends up, so that somebody can review it.
ui.mechanism.deadLetterQueue.model: Nothing. It is the only one of the eleven that moves no figure at all: not load, not latency, not propagation. A single rule reads it, QUEUE_NO_DLQ, and even that one waits until the queue has a consumer before firing. Moving no figure does not make it less important — it is the only defence against silent loss, and silent loss goes unsimulated precisely because it cannot be seen.
ui.mechanism.deadLetterQueue.avoid: There is no case where it is superfluous, but there is one where it misleads: enabling it processes nothing. What ends up in the dead letter queue is still not carried out, and if nobody reviews it the result is exactly what it was before, plus one more place where nobody looks.
ui.mechanism.cache.problem: A read that was already answered once does not need to be asked again. A cache in front retains most of them, and the database stops seeing them.
ui.mechanism.cache.model: What hits does not pass through: only load × (1 − h) continues behind it, and at the default 0.8 that is a fifth of what arrived. It lowers the target's load and, with it, its queueing factor — which is not linear, so taking load off something running nearly full is worth far more than it appears. A CDN starts at 0.9: static content is what caches best.
ui.mechanism.cache.formula:
load carrying on = load × (1 − h)
default h: 0.8 on a cache, 0.9 on a CDN
less load → lower utilization → lower queueing factor
ui.mechanism.cache.avoid: Do not place it in front of writes: a call declared as a write goes straight through it, and nothing is gained. Do not use it as a store: its data would live nowhere else, and a cache makes no durability guarantees (CACHE_AS_STORE). And the hit ratio is a declared value, not one the model measures: raising it to 0.99 on screen does not raise it in production, and a cache with few distinct keys or constantly changing data will not reach what the field claims.
ui.mechanism.readReplicas.problem: The other way to send the database fewer queries: not avoiding them, but spreading them across copies that only serve reads.
ui.mechanism.readReplicas.model: Every replica adds a full unit of capacity. A database is 200 rps per copy, and the copies are 1 + replicas + readReplicas. The simplification is worth knowing: the model has one capacity per component, so here a read replica raises the ceiling of the whole node, writes included. What it does distinguish is who reads what — MISSING_CACHE stands down for a database with read replicas, and the single-point-of-failure check counts only replicas.
ui.mechanism.readReplicas.avoid: Do not count them as redundancy: writes still go to a single machine, and the single-point-of-failure check counts replicas, not readReplicas. Outside the model they carry a cost this screen cannot show: every copy lags behind the primary, so what was just written may not yet be on the copy being read. And they are hardware: the no-new-hardware challenge forbids them along with instances, because its limit counts every copy of a component, replicas included.
ui.mechanism.rateLimit.problem: An entry point with no ceiling admits whatever arrives, and the components behind it pay for the surplus. The limit decides how much is admitted before it reaches anything.
ui.mechanism.rateLimit.model: It trims the load at the entry point itself: what gets in is the smaller of what arrives and the limit, and the rest never travels. This is the model's first non-linearity — it flattens the curve for everything behind it and, in exchange, discards requests. The discarded ones are counted: TRAFFIC_REJECTED fires when the limit rejects a substantial share of what was arriving.
ui.mechanism.rateLimit.formula:
admitted = min(load, rateLimit)
rejected = load − admitted
ui.mechanism.rateLimit.avoid: Do not use it as an answer to missing capacity: limiting is not scaling. Whatever does not get in is served by nobody, and those users count even when the diagram turns green. If a large share is being rejected, either capacity is missing behind the limit or the declared load is inflated, and the limit is only hiding which (TRAFFIC_REJECTED). Use it against a spike or a deliberate attack, not to make a warning disappear.
ui.mechanism.healthCheck.problem: A balancer spreads work across the copies it has. Without checking which ones are alive, it also sends work to the copy that has just gone down.
ui.mechanism.healthCheck.model: It only acts when the balancer has two or more targets of the same type. If one of those copies goes down, with a health check the group comes out Degraded and contained — the failure stops climbing — and without one it comes out Degraded and exposed. No rule reads it, so enabling it does not alter the score by a single point: all it changes is what is observed when an instance is taken down in simulation. That an architecture can withstand a failure better without scoring better is exactly what this tool sets out to teach.
ui.mechanism.healthCheck.formula:
two or more copies, one Down, health check   →   group Degraded (contained)
the same, no health check                    →   group Degraded, uncontained
a single copy behind it                      →   does nothing
ui.mechanism.healthCheck.avoid: Do not enable it with a single target behind the balancer: there is nothing to spread to and the model never reads it. Do not mistake it for redundancy: checking the health of one copy does not make it two. And outside the model it has a cost of its own: an overly aggressive check pulls out of rotation something that was merely slow, and then the survivor receives twice the load.
ui.mechanism.instances.problem: Capacity in this model is per copy. Declaring instances is what multiplies it, and it is also what prevents one copy going down from meaning the component going down.
ui.mechanism.instances.model: A node's capacity is its type's capacity times the number of instances: an API is 500 rps per copy, a service 300, a worker 200, a gateway 2,000, a cache or a broker 5,000, a load balancer 10,000. And from two upwards, the analyser stops seeing a single point of failure there. The stores carry no instances: a database declares replicas and a bucket declares replication. In this model, redundancy costs no latency and no coordination — two things that are paid for outside it —; it does cost money: every copy adds to the cost card, and excess has a warning of its own (OVERPROVISIONED).
ui.mechanism.instances.formula:
capacity = capacity per copy × instances
Api 500  ·  Service 300  ·  Worker 200 rps per copy
instances ≥ 2   →   no longer a single point of failure (SPOF)
ui.mechanism.instances.avoid: It is the shortcut, which is why some challenges forbid it: raising the number silences half the capacity warnings without any of them being understood. Before modifying it, check whether the surplus is load — a cache in front removes more than two copies behind — and bear in mind what the model does not charge for and what is paid for outside it: shared state, deployments, and a database that is still a single machine.
ui.model.headline: The figures the scoring uses
ui.model.lead: The database is the bottleneck by design: twenty-five times more fragile than a cache and ten times more than a gateway. That ratio is the whole reason the product's three lessons — put a cache in front, replicate, take it off the request path — have a visible effect without anyone tuning a number.
ui.model.loadFailed: The model could not be read.
ui.model.capacityLead: What one copy of each component withstands, what it costs to pass through it, and what it costs to keep it. The scale is logarithmic: every mark is worth ten times the previous one, so the three tiers — what stores, what computes, what the infrastructure absorbs — can be seen rather than explained.
ui.model.costNote: Cost is measured in units rather than euros, and the unit is defined by its anchor: a database costs 10. What teaches the lesson is not the cost column but the one beside it — how many rps one unit buys — because cost is not proportional to capacity: by capacity a cache is already twenty-five times a database; by cost, one hundred and twenty-five times. That is where “put a cache in front” stops being a recipe and becomes arithmetic.
ui.model.freeNote: The client and the external service are not components of yours: their bill never arrives, so they carry no cost and have no ratio.
ui.model.capacityNote: The three enormous capacities are not an oversight. The client is where load comes from, never where it piles up; and a bottleneck in the CDN or in the metrics pipeline is not a lesson this tool teaches.
ui.model.fixedNote: The external service is fixed: no configuration multiplies it because it is not a component of yours, and that is exactly what leaves a single possible answer: a fallback. Object storage is the other component whose capacity does not change, and that one is yours: its switch replicates the files, it does not raise the ceiling, so a saturated bucket has work taken off it rather than copies added to it.
ui.model.networkLead: What the hop itself costs, before any code runs, and the three figures that decide when the analysis begins to warn.
ui.model.hopNote: A call's protocol is determined by its two ends — SQL against a database, AMQP when a queue or a topic is at either end, HTTP for everything else — and it determines what the hop costs: the only part of the latency paid before any code runs.
ui.model.saturationBody: Past that share of its capacity a component becomes degraded and UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT is raised. Never worse: saturation brings nothing down by itself, it slows things down; the curve below shows by how much.
ui.model.unboundedBody: A call with no timeout is abandoned after {value:duration}. And since it never returns, the retries never happen: it is not "a timeout but worse", it is a different class of failure.
ui.model.hitRatioBody: What a cache and a CDN absorb when nothing declares otherwise. The gap between the two is the lesson: a CDN serves static content, which is the best-behaved cacheable traffic there is.
ui.model.queueingLead: Being close to the limit breaks nothing: it makes things slower. How much slower comes out of these two lines, and they are written to be computable by hand.
ui.model.rho: ρ is the load a component receives divided by what it can handle. At 100 % the two branches meet, and from there the cost grows linearly.
ui.model.queueingExample: A component at {utilization:percentPrecise} of its capacity makes a {base:duration} call cost {cost:durationPrecise}. Against a {timeout:duration} timeout that call expires, and the caller fails through TimeoutExceeded: that is how saturation brings down an entire architecture without killing a single component.
ui.node.Api.help: The synchronous interface the services expose: it takes a request and answers it. Placed in front of the data, it is where control over who asks for what belongs.
ui.node.Api.avoid: Do not chain one in front of another API of your own merely to add one more layer: every synchronous link adds its latency and its chance of failing to the same request (SYNC_CHAIN). And if it is the front door, declare whether identity is required; undeclared, the analysis can neither assume it nor rule it out.
ui.node.Cache.help: Keeps the reads that repeat close by. It absorbs the load that would otherwise reach the database whole.
ui.node.Cache.avoid: Do not use it as a store: if the components using it never reach a database or a bucket, what it holds is nowhere else, and a cache guarantees the preservation of nothing (CACHE_AS_STORE). One eviction, one restart or one cold node is enough to lose it.
ui.node.Cdn.help: The cache at the edge: it serves static content close to the user and absorbs most of the traffic before it reaches the origin. It is not a component of yours: it cannot be scaled; what can be decided is what happens when it is gone.
ui.node.Cdn.avoid: Do not place it in front of what is computed on every request: it absorbs static content, and anything that comes out different per user is still served by your own infrastructure. Nor should it be treated as one more replica: the day it becomes the single point of failure, the alternative is not to scale it, because it is not a component of yours, but to serve from the origin.
ui.node.Client.help: The outside, drawn: the users, the browser, whoever calls the system's door. What hangs from it is public; what does not is internal, and is no longer inferred from the shape of the graph.
ui.node.Client.avoid: Do not use it as a destination: the outside is where requests come from, not where they go, and an arrow from the system to somebody's browser is usually the response drawn as if it were a call (IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY). Nor should one be drawn per screen: what it declares is how much traffic comes in, not how many views there are.
ui.node.Database.help: Where the system keeps what has to survive a restart. Usually the first thing to saturate and the last thing to replicate without careful thought.
ui.node.Database.avoid: Do not place it at the end of every read: it is the most fragile thing in the model, and the whole read load ends up being its ceiling (MISSING_CACHE). And do not share it between services or leave it within reach of the outside: the first ties them together through the schema (SHARED_DATABASE), the second has nowhere to check who is calling (EXPOSED_DATABASE).
ui.node.ExternalService.help: A component that is not yours: it cannot be scaled, it cannot be given a corrective deployment, and there is no telling when it comes back. Every synchronous call to it needs to know what to answer when it is not there.
ui.node.ExternalService.avoid: Do not place it where a response is impossible without it: it cannot be scaled, it cannot be given a corrective deployment, and there is no telling when it comes back. A timeout does not silence it: it bounds the wait, but when it is over there is still no answer, and that is exactly the difference between EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK and MISSING_RESILIENCE.
ui.node.Gateway.help: The single door external traffic comes through. It checks who is calling and rejects at the entrance whatever exceeds the limit, which is where rejecting it is cheapest.
ui.node.Gateway.avoid: Do not place one in the middle of a call between two components of your own: it only checks what arrives from outside, so in there it is a hop that checks nothing. And if it is the only door, everything passes through it: with nothing beside it, it is the most expensive single point of failure in the diagram (SPOF).
ui.node.IdentityProvider.help: Where the question of who is calling is resolved. A door wired to it has already answered the authentication question, and on the synchronous path of every request it is the best-known single point of failure there is.
ui.node.IdentityProvider.avoid: Do not connect it behind the door: wiring it to an entry point is how it is declared that identity is required there, and connected to the inside it authenticates nothing. And if every entry delegates to it, its outage locks every user out at once (SPOF).
ui.node.LoadBalancer.help: Spreads requests across several equivalent instances. It is the usual answer to a single point of failure: if one instance goes down, the others keep answering.
ui.node.LoadBalancer.avoid: Do not place one in front of a single instance: sharing between one shares nothing, and the single point of failure has merely moved one component further up. Nor should its capacity be mistaken for the system's: what the whole thing withstands is added up by the instances behind it, and all it decides is which one gets each request; its own copies, if declared, only indicate that the door is not a single machine.
ui.node.ObjectStorage.help: For large files: images, video, attachments, backups. They are served from here instead of going through the database or a service's memory. Its redundancy is not counted in copies but declared: a replicated bucket keeps every file in more than one location.
ui.node.ObjectStorage.avoid: Do not use it for what has to be queried by field: it hands back whole files, and admits no queries. And it may not be a database, but it is still data: within reach of the outside, anyone who knows the address reads it (EXPOSED_DATABASE). It is not sized either: if it saturates, the answer is to take work off it —a CDN in front— and not to add copies, because the copies that can be declared provide redundancy, not capacity.
ui.node.Observability.help: Metrics, traces and logs: the place to look when something breaks. Without it, an incident is investigated by guessing.
ui.node.Observability.avoid: Do not draw it as one more component and leave it at that: the analysis evaluates each component's wire, not the presence of the component (NO_OBSERVABILITY). And do not send telemetry to it synchronously and without a timeout: that places the collector on the request path, and if it slows down the request waits with it.
ui.node.Queue.help: Decouples the requester from the worker: the message waits until somebody can take it. It breaks the synchronous chain, and with it the immediate spread of a failure.
ui.node.Queue.avoid: Do not draw one with no consumer: messages go in, none come out, the request is answered and the work it was trusted with is never carried out (QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER). And do not use it for what the user is waiting on at that moment: a queue decouples in time, it does not speed anything up.
ui.node.Topic.help: Publish-subscribe: every subscriber gets its own copy of every message, where a queue's consumers compete for each one. It is the difference between spreading work and broadcasting a fact — the base of event architectures.
ui.node.Topic.avoid: Do not use one when the message has a single recipient: a queue hands it to one consumer and a topic hands a copy to every subscriber, and the load model multiplies that copy by the fan-out. Broadcasting to nobody amounts to not broadcasting: with no subscribers the message is published and nobody receives it (QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER).
ui.node.Scheduler.help: The clock that fires background work. It gives workers a drawn origin and declares that the flow is not user traffic.
ui.node.Scheduler.avoid: Do not use it for what has to happen when the user requests it: it fires on a clock, and the analysis does not count what starts there as user traffic. And do not point it at a client or at a store: there is no work to fire against those (IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY).
ui.node.Service.help: A piece of business logic with a deployment of its own. The more pieces it needs to work, the harder it is to deploy, test and reason about on its own.
ui.node.Service.avoid: Do not turn it into the component that knows everything: the more it needs in order to answer, the harder it is to deploy on its own, and its availability is the product of all of theirs (HIGH_COUPLING). And do not have it write the same schema as another service: there the schema becomes the interface between the two (SHARED_DATABASE).
ui.node.Worker.help: Consumes work from a queue, off the request path. For whatever can take its time with nobody waiting at the other end.
ui.node.Worker.avoid: Do not place it on the request path: if whoever calls it waits for the answer, slow work has been placed where the clock is running, and the decoupling that justifies a worker no longer exists. Its source is a queue or a scheduler, not a synchronous call.

ui.rules.headline: Everything the analysis evaluates
ui.rules.lead: The analysis is deterministic: there is no language model behind it, but twenty-five rules that read the graph and its configuration. These are all of them, with the area they score in and whether they include an automatic fix.
ui.rules.noArchitecture: This is the plain catalogue. Open an architecture and each rule will also state what it found in it: whether it fired, whether it was passed, or whether it never applied; the last case indicates what the diagram is missing for the analysis to form an opinion.
ui.rules.noCoverage: This architecture was analysed before coverage existed, so the catalogue shows no states. Change something in the editor and return: the next analysis will include them.
ui.rules.stillTheCatalogue: The twenty-five rules are still here; what is missing is what each of them found in that architecture.
ui.rules.unknown: A rule the analyser already runs but this screen cannot explain yet.
ui.rules.whyNotAll: Where there is no fix button, it is not an omission: the correction has several legitimate answers, and choosing one automatically would remove exactly what the tool exists to teach. A single point of failure can be resolved by replicating, by balancing, or by no longer depending on it.
ui.rules.SPOF.detects: A component with no equivalent that the rest of the system hangs off. It does not count whoever calls it asynchronously, nor whoever already has a fallback answer. A balancer that spreads the load — over two components drawn, or over one that declares instances — is the way out, not a new single point of failure; a door, a balancer, a cache or a broker that declare two or more copies stop being one, and a store does it with its replicas —a bucket, with its replication—; and the CDN is not graded on it: its redundancy is the provider's.
ui.rules.TRAFFIC_REJECTED.detects: A door whose request limit turns away a substantial share of the traffic reaching it: a warning from one request in five, critical from half. Limiting is not scaling: the limit protects what is behind it, but nobody is serving those users. Either capacity is missing and the limit is low, or the declared load is inflated.
ui.rules.MISSING_RESILIENCE.detects: A synchronous call with no timeout; or with a timeout but no circuit breaker and no fallback towards a critical single point of failure. The fallback counts where the model counts it: a router's and a declared write's exist in the diagram alone, and do not lower the finding. On a declared write the button sets a timeout and a circuit breaker, never a fallback — a write that does not happen cannot be approximated — and the suggestion talks about a queue. The telemetry scrape (observability → component) does not count; a synchronous push towards observability does, and its fix is to make it asynchronous.
ui.rules.EXTERNAL_NO_FALLBACK.detects: There is a dependency on a third-party service with no declared alternative.
ui.rules.TIMEOUT_TOO_SHORT.detects: The timeout is shorter than the call itself: it always expires. It does not report on calls that land on — or wait for — an overloaded component: there the lesson is UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT, not the timeout. It carries no button: what makes a call take longer than its own timeout is the queue in front of it, so raising the number would only produce a slower answer, exactly what the challenge “The timeout that used to be enough” teaches to avoid.
ui.rules.TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG.detects: A timeout is a wait, not a limit: from 30 s upwards it protects exactly as much as none at all, because that is how long the model takes to give up on a call with no timeout. Critical if the call, with no circuit breaker and no fallback the model believes — a router's and a declared write's are not —, also lands on a single point of failure. The fix brings it down to twice what the call costs, never below 5 s.
ui.rules.RETRY_AMPLIFICATION.detects: Retries over several hops multiply onto the component that is already in difficulty.
ui.rules.QUEUE_NO_DLQ.detects: A queue with no dead letter queue: what cannot be processed has nowhere to go. It waits until the queue has a consumer: until then QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER is the one that reports.
ui.rules.CACHE_AS_STORE.detects: A cache whose users reach no database and no object storage: its data resides nowhere else, and a cache guarantees no preservation of it.
ui.rules.SYNC_CHAIN.detects: A long chain of synchronous calls linked end to end. If it ends in a read from a store, the suggestion is not a queue: it is shortening the path (reading from a cache or a replica, or merging the services in between). Declaring the last call as a write brings the queue advice back.
ui.rules.ASYNC_NO_QUEUE.detects: An asynchronous call between two working components with no queue or topic in between. Not waiting removes failure propagation, it does not give durability: if the target is away, the message is kept nowhere. An asynchronous push to observability does not count.
ui.rules.IMPLAUSIBLE_DEPENDENCY.detects: An arrow between two elements that cannot communicate: a store calling somebody, a component of yours calling the users, a CDN querying a database or publishing to a queue, a clock firing at a store, a gateway or a load balancer running SQL or declaring a fallback they do not have, a declared write with a fallback — what was not saved cannot be approximated. And the arrow that declares “nobody waits” where somebody has to: from the client, a gateway, a load balancer or a CDN; towards an identity provider; from a cache to its origin; towards a store when no write is declared — what nobody declares counts as a read, and reading is waiting for the data —; and the entry point that waits for nobody and queues nothing either, which has nothing to answer the outside with. Those are critical, because unticking “synchronous” is the cheapest way of making a failure vanish from the model. It speaks about the diagram and not about the architecture: while it is there, the rest of the panel describes a system other than yours.
ui.rules.HIGH_COUPLING.detects: A component piling up too many dependencies. A gateway or a balancer is measured with twice the margin: spreading the load is their job.
ui.rules.QUEUE_NO_CONSUMER.detects: A queue somebody publishes to and nobody consumes from: messages go in and do not come out. The consumer is whoever receives the arrow from the queue; a worker pointing at the queue is publishing.
ui.rules.SHARED_DATABASE.detects: Two or more different services on the same database or object storage: the schema is the interface between them. Only Service-type ones count, and the replicas of one — the components of the same type behind the same balancer — count as one. It reads the access declared on each call: if two or more write, the lesson is the writers'; if at most one can write, the readers'.
ui.rules.UNDERSIZED_COMPONENT.detects: It receives more requests than it can serve, or it is right at the limit. In a database, the declared writes only have the primary and its full replicas: read replicas do not write, and the finding says so when it is the writes that overflow. A bucket is the only one that is not sized: it has no copies to declare —its replication provides redundancy, not capacity—, so there the advice is to take work off it.
ui.rules.MISSING_CACHE.detects: Direct queries to the database with no cache and no read replica. A call declared as a write does not count, and the replicas of a service count as one.
ui.rules.MISSING_CDN.detects: A door with high traffic and no CDN in front of it. The edge is the cheapest way to scale; the warning raises a question rather than asserting an error: if the traffic is purely dynamic and there is nothing to cache, leave the diagram as it is.
ui.rules.UNAUTHENTICATED_ENTRY.detects: An exposed entry point with no authentication and data behind it — a database or an object storage. Declared or not, it is a critical: a door nobody has vouched for is open until proven otherwise. It only asks the doors traffic reaches — declared on them or upstream — or that hang from a drawn Client: two components and an arrow with nobody calling them are not an open door, and the rule does not apply. Wiring the door to an identity provider counts as declaring it. And any component of yours taking traffic from outside with no way to check who is calling — a worker, a cache, a queue, a topic — is a warning on its own: the lesson is to place a door in front of it.
ui.rules.EXPOSED_DATABASE.detects: The data — a database or an object storage — is reached without going through any door: an API, a gateway or a service. With a Client drawn, “from outside” is exactly what hangs off it; with no Client, a Worker, a Scheduler or observability never count as “outside”. The bucket a CDN serves does not count: it is the served bucket, not the public one.
ui.rules.NO_RATE_LIMIT.detects: A door — an API or a gateway — that traffic reaches and that does not limit how many requests it takes.
ui.rules.NO_OBSERVABILITY.detects: A component with no wire to the observability, in either direction: one warning per component, so the area improves as components are wired. If none is observed, a single critical instead of the warnings: the system is blind — and having the component unwired does not avoid it; the first wire turns it into warnings. With the component drawn, each component also keeps its “connect” button as an informational finding, which does not subtract: the blindness is charged once and the correction is still one click away. It does not ask the Client, an external service, a CDN or an identity provider: they are not components of yours to instrument.
ui.rules.OVERPROVISIONED.detects: A component with more copies than the declared load needs, while using less than a fifth of what it has set up. It never proposes going below two: the second copy is not capacity, it is what takes it out of being a single point of failure. It does not report until somebody declares traffic: with no load there is no telling what is spare. It is a warning while the excess is moderate and a critical from four times the copies the load needs: past that, paying over the odds stops being caution.

web.home.headline: Backend architecture: building systems, inducing failure, understanding why.
web.home.subhead: Bondstone analyses the system as drawn and reports what fails, why, and on which component. The failure of any component can be induced deliberately, in order to observe how far it propagates. Once the problem is corrected, the measurement is repeated.
web.home.condition: No account and no registration. Every architecture is a link: whoever receives it can consult it, induce failures in it, and obtain a copy.
web.home.audience: Intended for backend developers who have seen a system go down and want to understand why.

web.home.loop.title: Four stages, each with a result
web.home.loop.1.text: Sixteen component types; at least one rule evaluates each of them. No element of the palette is decorative.
web.home.loop.2.text: A score out of 100 that can be traced back to its reason: what occurs, why it is relevant, and on which component. The analysis also states what it was unable to evaluate.
web.home.loop.3.text: A component can be stopped, degraded, or brought down together with its entire zone. The result states what falls with it, how many requests are lost, and at what traffic volume it stops responding.
web.home.loop.4.text: A timeout, a queue, a replica. The same scenario and the same drawing: any change in the result comes solely from the correction introduced.
web.home.criterion.title: The full criterion is public
web.home.criterion.deterministic: Deterministic: the same architecture always produces the same result. The 25 rules, capacities, latencies and thresholds are published and open to discussion.
web.home.criterion.teaching: A teaching model, deliberately so: no simulated time, no probability, and every figure in the open. Its purpose is learning, not the measurement of production systems.
web.home.criterion.noAi: No AI involved. What the product states is true for the model, and the model is published. For a second opinion, the findings can be exported with a closing prompt and taken to whichever LLM is preferred.
web.home.challenges.title: 23 challenges posed as incidents
web.home.challenges.lead: Each one includes a faulty architecture, a situation, the requirements the engine checks, three hints, and the reference solution once it is passed. They are ordered: each challenge builds on the previous one.

web.home.notWhat: Bondstone is not a diagramming tool, nor a production simulator, nor a course. It is an environment in which architecture decisions are taken and their consequences observed. No account, no leaderboard, and no AI involved.

web.legal.title: Legal notice & privacy
web.legal.lead: What is kept when you use Bondstone, what for, and on what terms the service is offered.
web.legal.who.title: Controller
web.legal.who.p1: Bondstone is a personal project by Juan Puerta Gil de Gómez, backend developer, with no company behind it. He is responsible for the processing described on this page. For any question about it, write to juanpuertagildegomez@gmail.com.
web.legal.data.title: What is kept
web.legal.data.lead: Three things, each with its reason. Nothing else leaves this application.
web.legal.data.arch.label: The architectures
web.legal.data.arch.body: They are stored on the server anonymously, tied to no person, and identified solely by their link: whoever knows it can view them, and whoever holds the edit link can modify and delete them. For that reason, avoid writing personal data in component names.
web.legal.data.ip.label: The IP address
web.legal.data.ip.body: It is used to cap the number of requests a single client can make within an interval and keep the service available to everyone; the limiter holds it in memory only for as long as that interval lasts. As on any web server, it also appears in the access log, which rotates and overwrites itself: it is not archived, not copied to any other system, and not used for anything else. The legal basis is the legitimate interest in protecting the service.
web.legal.data.local.label: Progress and preferences
web.legal.data.local.body: Passed challenges, recently opened work, language and appearance are kept in your browser's local storage and are never sent to the server. They are removed by clearing the site's data from the browser itself.
web.legal.none.title: What there is not
web.legal.none.lead: What other applications take for granted and does not exist here.
web.legal.none.accounts.label: Accounts
web.legal.none.accounts.body: There is no sign-up and no log-in. You can draw, analyse and pass challenges without identifying yourself.
web.legal.none.email.label: Email
web.legal.none.email.body: None is requested to use the service. The address on this page is for writing to whoever maintains it, not for signing up.
web.legal.none.cookies.label: Cookies
web.legal.none.cookies.body: None is set. Local storage is used solely so that the application works and remembers your preferences — the use the regulations exempt from consent — which is why no cookie banner is shown.
web.legal.none.third.label: Third parties
web.legal.none.third.body: There are no analytics, no advertising, and no external services watching your browsing.
web.legal.none.closing: The only data leaving the browser are the drawings you choose to save and the requests needed to analyse them.
web.legal.rights.title: Your rights
web.legal.rights.p1: You can delete an architecture at any time from the editor, using its edit link, and it disappears from the server. As there are no accounts, there is no data tied to you to consult, rectify or export beyond the drawings identified by their links.
web.legal.rights.p2: If you believe some processing is not correct, you can raise it at that address or lodge a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD).
web.legal.terms.title: Terms of use
web.legal.terms.p1: Bondstone is a free service for teaching purposes. The analysis, scores and simulations illustrate design principles with a deliberately simplified model; they are neither professional advice nor a prediction of how any real system will behave.
web.legal.terms.p2: The service is offered as is, with no guarantee of availability or of indefinite retention of what is saved. Export whatever you want to keep.
web.legal.terms.p3: What you draw is yours. By saving it, you allow it to be stored and shown to whoever holds the link. Any unlawful content, or content that abuses the service, may be removed.
web.legal.terms.p4: These terms may change; the date in the header indicates the latest version.

editor.legend.badgesNote: One dot per component named by a finding, in the ink of its severity: critical or warning. Enabled with “{toggle}”.
editor.legend.containedNote: A ring and, inside the component, the name of the mechanism that stopped the cascade. It marks the difference between three components down and seven.
editor.legend.highlightedNote: A ring around the components and calls of the finding open in the panel.
editor.legend.degradedNote: Still in service, but responding worse, and that degradation propagates upstream.
editor.legend.downNote: It has stopped responding, and the call reaching it is drawn dashed.
editor.legend.healthyNote: No mark: healthy components are drawn as always.
editor.legend.loadNote: The proportion of its capacity the component uses under the declared load. The notch marks {value:percent}, the point at which the analysis begins to warn; beyond capacity, the bar changes ink again.
editor.legend.zoneDownNote: The frame changes when everything it contains is down. This is what the failure of an entire zone looks like, as opposed to that of a single component: the fault affects everything sharing the location at once.
